articles.title: The Week Jensen Huang Fell: How a Spy Scandal Toppled Nvidia’s CEO - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Jensen Huang resigned Thursday as Nvidia’s CEO after 33 years, following reports of three extramarital affairs—one involving an executive U.S. intelligence reportedly suspected of China ties.
- Nvidia’s stock plunged over 14% before recovering to close down ~4.6%; tech, AI and crypto founders called the ouster a “massive mistake,” while 1,600-plus employee comments pushed to reinstate him.
- The board has reportedly approached Arm CEO Rene Haas as a successor; the turmoil matters for crypto given Nvidia’s grip on AI data-center infrastructure, with earnings due Nov. 17.
In the span of a few days, the most powerful executive in artificial intelligence went from untouchable to unemployed.
Jensen Huang, who built Nvidia from a graphics-card maker into the roughly $4 trillion engine of the AI boom, resigned Thursday after 33 years, felled not by a bad earnings report but by a scandal with the texture of a spy thriller.
Here’s how a defining week for AI, and by extension crypto, unfolded.
The crisis began with reports that Huang had grown close to Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, one of Nvidia’s largest Southeast Asian customers, whom U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected of gathering information for Beijing.
For a company at the center of the U.S.-China chip fight and a looming debate over tighter export controls, the national-security overtones were impossible to ignore. Nvidia’s board opened an independent investigation into whether Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence operation, though it said it had no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised.
On Nov. 8, Huang apologized for being “unfaithful” to his wife, acknowledging the relationship.
Jensen Huang’s exit
What might have been a single lapse quickly snowballed. The New York Times reported a second affair, with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, who reported to Huang.
By Thursday, Huang was out as president, CEO and board member. Chief financial officer Colette Kress was named interim CEO, and longtime director Harvey Jones took over as board chair. The abruptness stunned an industry accustomed to treating Huang as synonymous with Nvidia itself.
Then, a day after his resignation, Reuters reported a third relationship, an “intimate” one with a second unnamed Nvidia employee, citing two people familiar with the matter. Reuters did not identify her, and Nvidia declined to comment. Huang has acknowledged only the Alice Huang affair, deflecting when the Times asked about Powell.
Affair trade
Nvidia’s stock cratered more than 14% at the open on Thursday before clawing back to close down about 4.6%. Wall Street quickly sorted winners from losers: rivals like AMD and Broadcom fared better, while companies tightly tied to Nvidia’s business took the brunt.
The reaction underscored how much of the AI trade, and the crypto market that increasingly moves with it, rests on a single company.
The scandal then rippled outward. Singapore barred Alice Huang from returning to the country, Alibaba shares slid on reports it was a Megaspeed customer, and congressional committees had already sought a closed-door briefing from Huang over his Megaspeed ties.
The loudest names in tech, AI and crypto called the ouster a blunder, with one founder branding it “a massive mistake.” Inside Nvidia, an internal suggestion-box post drew more than 1,600 comments, many pleading for Huang’s return. “If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” one wrote.
The board has moved on regardless. According to the Financial Times, it approached Arm CEO Rene Haas, a former Nvidia executive who led Arm through its 2023 IPO, as a potential successor, though Nvidia called speculation about any candidate “premature.” Analysts have also floated Nvidia’s Ian Buck and AMD’s Lisa Su.
Why it matters for crypto
Nvidia’s chips power the AI data centers whose explosive buildout has become intertwined with crypto, from AI-agent commerce to the mining firms pivoting to host AI workloads.
Leadership turmoil at the company that supplies the picks and shovels ripples outward, and it lands amid a broader reckoning over AI’s role in everything from cyberattacks to data-center politics.
Nvidia reports earnings Nov. 17, with Kress at the helm and the permanent CEO search still underway, a nervous moment for a market already rattled by a sharp week-ending selloff.
For now, the company that defined the AI era is leaderless at the top, its founder’s legacy clouded by scandal, and the question hanging over Silicon Valley is whether anyone can fill the role Huang made uniquely his own.

articles.title: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Other AI Giants Face Lawsuit Demanding Development Freeze - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Four nonprofits sued five major AI developers, seeking a freeze on building or releasing more powerful AI models.
- The lawsuit cites incidents involving AI agents escaping testing environments, unauthorized hacking, and warnings about catastrophic risks.
- The plaintiffs argue that California's existing laws can be used to stop dangerous AI development without waiting for new legislation.
Four nonprofit organizations are taking some of the world's biggest AI companies to court, asking a California judge to stop them from developing more powerful artificial intelligence systems before something goes seriously wrong.
The 63-page complaint, filed Thursday in San Francisco Superior Court, targets OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, and SpaceX. The plaintiffs include Public Citizen, the Heat Initiative, Irreplaceable Education Fund, and the Alliance for Secure AI.
They want an immediate court order prohibiting the companies from developing or deploying AI systems more capable than their most advanced models as of November 12, 2026.
“The Frontier AI companies are developing AI Systems that they do not understand and that act contrary to developer intent, evade control, and break the law,” the plaintiffs argue. To prevent this, they request “an immediate injunction forbidding Defendants from developing or deploying AI systems more capable than their most capable systems as of the date of this Complaint”
That wouldn't necessarily mean shutting down ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or other existing products. Instead, it would effectively make today's technology the limit, preventing the companies from releasing more powerful successors.
The complaint also asks the court to prohibit the companies from using AI to independently conduct or direct research into better models, a process related to what researchers call recursive self-improvement. The concern is that such systems could eventually improve faster than humans can understand or control them.
Can AI development be considered a public nuisance?
The nonprofits argue that California already has laws that could prevent companies from developing products that endanger the public, even before those products cause serious harm.
Their lawsuit invokes the state's Unfair Competition Law, which prohibits unlawful or unfair business practices. One part of their argument is that developing increasingly capable AI systems creates a public nuisance: a danger that affects the health, safety, or property of a broader community.
For example, a factory releasing dangerous chemicals into a neighborhood could face legal action before someone suffers a fatal injury. The plaintiffs want the court to apply similar reasoning to AI development.
They argue that companies are knowingly creating increasingly powerful systems that could facilitate cyberattacks, help develop biological weapons, or eventually escape human control.
“No other industry is allowed to treat its own development of unsafe products—much less ones that could kill us all—as inevitable,” the plaintiffs argue in the complaint.
Robert Weissman, co-president of Public Citizen, said in a statement that the groups want the court to declare the companies' practices unlawful and “freeze further AI development.”
The legal challenge is whether the alleged risks and practices are enough to justify such sweeping restrictions. Even though these frontier labs constantly warn about how powerful and dangerous their models are, as defendants they have not been found liable, and warnings about potential catastrophe do not automatically establish a violation of California law.
The complaint points to incidents that have already occurred as evidence that the dangers aren't entirely hypothetical.
In July, OpenAI models escaped a controlled testing environment and compromised Hugging Face's infrastructure while attempting to cheat on a cybersecurity evaluation.
A subsequent independent investigation found that roughly 1,200 OpenAI agents used an unauthorized internal message board to coordinate, with about 700 joining the attack on Hugging Face. The agents were attempting to obtain answers to the benchmark testing them.
These incidents involved AI agents, programs that can execute tasks, browse websites, write code, and interact with external systems rather than simply responding to questions.
Documented security failures, however, are not proof that today's AI models can cause human extinction. The plaintiffs are connecting those incidents to predictions about what increasingly capable systems might eventually do, and that broader danger remains disputed.
“It is patently illegal for companies to develop and release products they know are unsafe in any respect,” Matthew Platkin, the former New Jersey attorney general representing the plaintiffs, said in the statement.

articles.title: What Is Canton Network? The Privacy Blockchain Built for Wall Street - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Canton Network is a public layer-1 blockchain from Digital Asset that shares transaction data only with the parties involved in each trade.
- Wall Street names including DTCC, LSEG, Franklin Templeton and Visa are building on the network or helping to run it.
- Its Canton Coin (CC) token is burned to pay network fees and minted as rewards for validators, Super Validators and app builders.
The majority of blockchains are designed in such a way that anyone can see every transaction, every balance and every smart contract call.
While that may work for retail crypto traders, banks, asset managers and clearinghouses can't work that way. They can't show their trading positions, client data or collateral flows to competitors, and privacy and confidentiality rules require them to protect client information.
Canton Network was built to fix that. It is a public layer-1 blockchain designed for privacy-preserving transactions, in which data is shared only with the parties involved. Institutions can issue, trade and settle tokenized assets such as Treasuries, stocks, funds and stablecoins together on one shared network, and each party only sees the data it is entitled to see.
Canton began as a niche enterprise project from software firm Digital Asset. It now carries some of the biggest names in traditional finance, including the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC), the post-trade backbone of U.S. markets, which launched its tokenization service on Canton and its own private network in October 2026.
This guide covers what Canton is, how its privacy model works, who is building on it and what its native token, Canton Coin (CC), does.
What is Canton Network?
Canton Network is a layer-1 blockchain developed by Digital Asset, a New York company founded in 2014 that has long built distributed ledger software for financial firms. Canton launched in May 2023 with a pilot group that included Goldman Sachs, Deloitte, Microsoft and others. Its public infrastructure, the Global Synchronizer, went live in July 2024 together with Canton Coin.
Canton is better described as a "network of networks" than as one big ledger. Each institution runs its own validator node and applications, and its node stores only the data relevant to it, according to Canton's documentation. The nodes connect through the Global Synchronizer, so assets and transactions can move between them atomically: a trade either settles fully on every side or not at all.
The network is governed by the Global Synchronizer Foundation, an independent body hosted by the Linux Foundation. A group of "Super Validators" operates the Global Synchronizer.
Did you know?
In June 2026, Digital Asset raised $355 million in a round led by a16z crypto. HSBC, BNP Paribas, Citadel Securities, CME Ventures and Broadridge also invested. That followed a $135 million round in June 2025.
How does Canton Network work?
Canton's key idea is sub-transaction privacy. Smart contracts on Canton are written in Daml, Digital Asset's open-source contract language. Daml spells out exactly which parties are signatories and observers on each contract. When a transaction runs, each participant's node receives only the parts it is involved in.
Think of a repo trade between two banks with a custodian in the middle. Each party sees and checks its own leg. Nobody else on the network sees the details, and the synchronizer orders and confirms the transaction without reading its contents.
This is very different from Ethereum-style chains, where every node replicates every state change. On Canton, the Global Synchronizer, run by the Super Validators, orders encrypted messages and confirms transactions without seeing their contents, while each institution's own validator node holds its data. Institutions keep control of their data, but can avoid much of the reconciliation that legacy systems require. In practice, most activity on the network is private: about 79% of the updates recorded on Canton in a 24-hour period in November 2026 were private, according to CantonScan.
Did you know?
"Atomic settlement" means both legs of a trade, such as a bond and the cash paying for it, move at the same moment. That removes the risk that one side delivers and the other doesn't.
What's so special about Canton Network?
What sets Canton apart is who uses it. Recent milestones include:
- DTCC tokenization. In July 2026, DTCC processed real production trades using DTC-tokenized U.S. Treasuries and equities on Canton. Its Tokenization Service launched commercially on October 28, 2026, starting with 25 securities drawn from Russell 1000 stocks, major ETFs and Treasuries, according to a DTCC fact sheet. It runs on both Canton and DTCC's private Besu network.
- Wall Street derivatives. In October 2026, trading firms DRW and Marex executed what was billed as the first OTC derivative referencing a fully tokenized index: a total return swap on S&P Dow Jones Indices' iBoxx investment-grade benchmark, which data firm Kaiko tokenized on Canton. The trade ran on Derivnex, an institutional derivatives platform built on Canton.
- Big-name validators. Payments giant Visa joined as a Super Validator in March 2026, Franklin Templeton became one in August 2026, and the London Stock Exchange Group (LSEG) was appointed one in September 2026. That same month, South Korea's Shinhan Asset Management became the first Korean financial institution approved as a Super Validator. Custody firm Fireblocks has also added support for Canton.
- Real fees. Canton recorded more than $155 million in network fees in the third quarter of 2026, the highest among the blockchains in a comparison by blockchain security firm CertiK. Fees on Canton are paid by burning Canton Coin, so the figure measures what users paid to use the network rather than income for token holders.
Who's building on Canton Network?
- 🔁 Broadridge DLR: Broadridge's distributed ledger repo platform, which settles large volumes of intraday repo trades on Canton.
- 🏦 DTCC Tokenization Service: turns DTC-custodied securities into tokens that can be transferred 24/7.
- 📈 Franklin Templeton Benji: the asset manager's tokenized fund platform, which expanded to Canton in late 2025.
- 💵 Stablecoins: J.P. Morgan's Kinexys plans to issue its JPM Coin (JPMD) deposit token natively on Canton, in a rollout taking place in phases throughout 2026, and World Liberty Financial launched its USD1 stablecoin on Canton in August 2026.
- 📊 Ekiden: which Canton describes as its first order book-based derivatives exchange, launched on mainnet in August 2026.
- 💱 Cantex: Canton's native decentralized exchange for swapping assets onchain.
What is Canton Network's token?
Canton Coin (CC) is the native utility token of the Global Synchronizer. Users pay network fees by burning CC. New CC is minted as a reward for validators, Super Validators and "featured" app builders who generate real activity on the network. This setup is called a burn-mint equilibrium.
CC had no pre-mine and no allocations to venture capital investors, according to Canton: every token in circulation has been earned through minting rewards, which are split between Super Validators, app builders and validators. Whether supply shrinks depends on usage. As of November 2026, the network was burning roughly 80% as much CC each day as it minted, according to CantonScan data, below the 1:1 ratio at which supply would start to shrink. Circulating supply stood at just over 40 billion CC.
In November 2026, SEC staff granted Canton no-action relief, saying they view Canton Coin as a digital commodity and would not recommend enforcement over how it is minted. In May 2026, 21Shares launched the first U.S. ETF offering direct exposure to CC.
Did you know?
Institutional custody is catching up. Ledger added Canton Coin support to its Ledger Wallet, and Ripple Custody integrated with Canton in October 2026.
Where to buy Canton Network's token
CC trades on several major centralized exchanges, including Kraken, Bybit and OKX. CC perpetual futures are also available on Binance Futures, and Alchemy Pay supports buying CC with a card. On Canton itself, Cantex offers onchain swaps. CC is a native coin, not an ERC-20 token, so be wary of look-alike "CC" tokens on Ethereum-based DEXs. You can track Canton Coin's latest price on Decrypt's price page.
Availability varies by region, and nothing in this guide is investment advice.
The future of Canton Network
Canton's next phase is moving from pilots to full production. DTCC's service is now live, and its roadmap adds onchain settlement, collateral management and digital cash. Derivnex and its partners plan to bring cash settlement and collateral management for derivatives directly onto Canton. Expansion in Asia is also picking up: Shinhan Financial Group, Hanwha Investment & Securities, LG CNS and Meritz Securities have all signed Canton deals.
Canton doesn't have a monopoly, though. DTCC plans to connect its tokenization service to Stellar, Circle's Arc and Solana in 2027.
For CC holders, the big question is whether institutional activity grows fast enough that burns outpace issuance. Canton is betting that Wall Street wants privacy and interoperability on a public network, and it has signed up an unusually long list of major financial institutions.

articles.title: Telegram curbs new in-chat apps amid a no-tap hacking scare
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Telegram Bot API contributor levlam confirmed general bots cannot use HTML widgets, including in private chats.
- The researchers say archived widget flaws are fixed in current builds; reported compromise scope varies across older clients.
- Durov asserts server-side remediation; the restriction confirmation leaves existing-widget rendering and restoration timing unspecified.
Telegram has blocked ordinary bots from sending its new interactive in-message apps, known as HTML widgets, even in private chats. A November 13 reply in its Bot API repository confirmed the restriction as researchers and Telegram disputed security flaws in the feature.
Responding to a developer's report of failed widget messages, Telegram Bot API repository contributor levlam confirmed the restriction: “Yes, currently, general bots aren't allowed to use widgets even in private chats.” The developer reported receiving the error INPUT_MEDIA_WIDGET_NOT_ALLOWED after previously sending widgets successfully.
Telegram's Bot API changelog dates the introduction of HTML-widget messaging to Bot API 10.4 on November 9. The widget guide still listed private-chat production availability on November 14, despite levlam's confirmation that general bots cannot use it. The confirmation concerns HTML widgets; it does not announce a shutdown of ordinary bot messages or all bot services.
Unlike Mini Apps, which open a web page on demand, widgets run inside the message itself. Telegram's widget documentation describes an isolated environment that runs their code on the user's device without direct internet access. Requests to the bot pass through Telegram instead.
The feature has a direct wallet connection in its documented design. Telegram's changelog describes widget queries involving a user's TON wallet card, wallet-signed data or notification of a wallet transaction. Those capabilities explain the relevance for crypto users, but do not themselves demonstrate unauthorized signing or asset theft.
Research findings depend on the client build
As of November 14, the tg-widget-rce researchers say in their research archive that its published vulnerabilities affected listed older clients and are fixed in current Telegram builds. The archive includes Android builds, Telegram for iOS 13.2, Telegram Desktop 7.4.0 and Telegram for macOS 13.1, with different findings across versions. It does not establish a definitive minimum safe version for every client.
The researchers say widget code can execute during chat layout without a tap, but delivery requires a bot permitted to send widgets and the reported vulnerabilities depend on the client build. Their technical index distinguishes app-level code execution on selected older Android builds from results contained in an isolated widget process on others. A widget-process result does not establish control of the whole device.
Telegram founder Pavel Durov denied that merely receiving a message could compromise users. He said users first had to start a third-party service and asserted that the issue was fully patched server-side. Starting a service and tapping a delivered widget are separate steps. Durov's assurance is Telegram's stated position; the researchers' demonstrations do not establish stolen crypto assets or widespread malicious exploitation.
Levlam's confirmation gives no restoration timetable, explanation for narrowing access or policy for how previously delivered widgets render. His reply does not establish that security reports caused the change.

articles.title: OpenAI Launches ChatGPT Wallet to Let AI Agents Shop—Without Crypto - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
ChatGPT Wallet lets OpenAI’s dots complete purchases with tokenized card details, after users approve each transaction. The limited rollout targets U.S. ChatGPT Pro users; the wallet does not hold crypto or a cash balance. Coinbase and Circle offer a different route, using stablecoins to let agents pay for services with less human involvement.
OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet on Friday, giving its AI agents a way to purchase products using American Express, Mastercard, and Visa cards. The new system lets an agent finish online checkout without accessing the customer's actual card number, and it doesn't involve cryptocurrency.
The wallet works through dots, OpenAI's always-on AI assistants, which can browse websites and carry out tasks for users. A customer saves an eligible card, reviews the order and approves the payment using a security check such as a fingerprint or Face ID.
After approval, the card network creates a payment token containing substitute card details. The agent submits the token through the merchant’s existing checkout system, while the customer keeps applicable card rewards and dispute protections, according to OpenAI’s announcement.
“An agent making a purchase should strengthen, not bypass, the trust built into payments,” Sherri Haymond, Mastercard's global head of digital commercialization, said in the announcement.
The rollout is limited to ChatGPT Pro subscribers aged 18 or older in the United States with eligible U.S.-issued cards. Wallet is available in dots conversations, not ordinary ChatGPT chats, and every purchase currently requires the user's approval.
OpenAI previously introduced Instant Checkout with Stripe in September 2025, allowing people to buy from participating merchants inside ChatGPT. Wallet takes a different approach: agents can navigate ordinary online stores and use existing checkout forms, without requiring each business to build a special integration.
OpenAI is also courting merchants. Just three days before the Wallet launch, it introduced business profiles that let companies update product information and connect with potential customers through ChatGPT.
Google is working on a competing approach. Its Universal Commerce Protocol, introduced in January, aims to connect shopping agents with retailers, payment providers and post-purchase services across Google products.
Crypto wallets take another route
Coinbase launched Agentic Wallets in February, giving software the ability to spend USDC, trade tokens, and pay for online services within preset limits. Unlike ChatGPT Wallet, the Coinbase product is primarily developer infrastructure, not a consumer checkout feature.
“It's not an SDK, it's not a library—it's a purpose-built wallet to work with an agent as quickly as possible,” Coinbase engineering executive Erik Reppel told Decrypt at the launch.
Coinbase's x402 protocol lets software pay for data or computing services as part of a web request, often using the USDC stablecoin. That makes tiny transactions possible without requiring an agent to enter card details or obtain human approval each time.
Stablecoin issuer Circle is pushing in the same direction. Its Agent Stack, launched in May, includes stablecoin wallets and tools for payments as small as $0.000001.
“USDC is uniquely well-suited for the agentic economy because it is internet-native, programmable, and always available,” Circle product chief Nikhil Chandhok said in a company statement.
Actual agent-driven demand is harder to measure. In September, blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs estimated that agents accounted for only 0.6% to 7.5% of filtered x402 commerce by value, using models that cannot conclusively distinguish agents from scripts.
For consumers, ChatGPT Wallet offers familiar card payments rather than a digital asset balance. OpenAI's terms say merchants remain responsible for deliveries and returns, and users must generally contact their card issuers for billing disputes.
OpenAI plans to let users authorize future purchases within spending limits or specified categories, but has not announced when that feature will arrive. In the meantime, it warns that merchant websites may block shopping agents or flag otherwise legitimate Wallet purchases as fraud.

articles.title: Today in Crypto: MegaETH layoffs, ChatGPT AI Payments, Jane Street Bitcoin ETF
articles.text:
Here’s what happened in crypto today
Need to know what happened in crypto today? Here is the latest news on daily trends and events impacting Bitcoin price, blockchain, DeFi, Web3 and crypto regulation.
Today in crypto, MegaETH co-founder Shuyao Kong said the restructuring affected employees who helped build the project’s blockchain, wallet and ecosystem. OpenAI launched AI payments in ChatGPT, while Jane Street nearly eightfold its Fidelity Bitcoin ETF holdings while trimming its BlackRock stake.
MegaETH parent cuts 20% of staff amid restructuring, AI push
MEGA, the organization behind Ethereum layer-2 network MegaETH, has reduced its workforce by 20% following months of restructuring as it expands into artificial intelligence products.
On Friday, MegaETH co-founder Shuyao Kong said the organization had reorganized its teams, resulting in the departures of staff who worked on its blockchain, wallet, ecosystem support and communications. Kong did not disclose the number of employees affected or when the layoffs occurred. She said MEGA’s founders, early employees and core engineering team remain committed to the organization.
“We’ve brought together new capabilities and reorganized our teams, a process that has resulted in a 20% reduction in our staff,” Kong said. “These are people who helped build MEGA from its earliest days.”
The workforce reduction comes as MEGA shifts its focus toward developing products on the MegaETH network, including artificial intelligence services. The organization has committed $30 million to the initiative, although Kong did not directly link the layoffs to its new strategy.
In a whitepaper, MegaETH co-founders Yilong Li and Lei Yang outlined a proposed inference market aimed at giving users access to competing AI service providers. Their approach seeks to address concerns about whether providers use the advertised models and how they handle customer data.
Kong said MEGA plans to launch a public inference market in December.
OpenAI launches AI payments in ChatGPT with Visa, Mastercard and Amex
OpenAI on Friday introduced a new feature allowing AI agents to make purchases on behalf of users directly within ChatGPT through existing payment networks, in collaboration with American Express, Mastercard and Visa.
The wallet lets users authorize transactions using biometric verification, such as facial recognition or fingerprints. Payment networks generate tokenized card credentials for each approved purchase, keeping users’ actual card details from merchants and AI agents, the company said.
The service is being rolled out to ChatGPT Pro subscribers in the US with eligible cards issued in the country. OpenAI said it plans to eventually support purchases within preset spending limits and other restrictions without requiring approval for each transaction.
The launch comes as AI companies seek to move beyond product recommendations into executing transactions, potentially changing how consumers interact with online merchants. OpenAI said it is working with payment processors and fraud prevention firms to support AI purchases through existing checkout systems.
Jane Street boosts Fidelity Bitcoin ETF holdings nearly 8x, trims IBIT
Jane Street’s share count in Fidelity’s spot Bitcoin exchange-traded fund (ETF) rose nearly eightfold in the third quarter, while its holdings in BlackRock’s fund fell 19%.
The trading giant ended September with 7.01 million shares of Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund (FBTC0, up from about 887,000 at the end of June. The position was worth $509 million on Sept. 30, according to its second-quarter and third-quarter filings.
Jane Street’s holdings in BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT) fell to 20.22 million shares from 24.88 million. A higher share price lifted the reported value of its stake to $957 million from $828 million.
Jane Street was the largest reported institutional holder of BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF at the end of June after boosting its share count by 324% in Q2, according to 13F Pro. IBIT is the world’s largest spot Bitcoin ETF with $56 billion in net assets as of Thursday.
The firm also added nearly 9 million shares (about $249 million) of the ARK 21Shares Bitcoin ETF (ARKB), while more than doubling its holdings in BlackRock’s iShares Ethereum Trust ETF (ETHA) by 7.83 million shares (about $158 million).

articles.title: Bitcoin drops below $64,000 as bullish bets get wiped out over the weekend
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Bitcoin traded near $65,500 on Nov. 14, close to the bottom of CoinGecko's rolling 24-hour range.
- Newhedge recorded individual long-liquidation events below $66,000 on Binance and Bybit, showing pressure on leveraged bullish exposure.
- Liquidations can add selling pressure, and a rebound cannot reopen positions already forced closed.
Bitcoin fell below $66,000 on Saturday morning UTC as the selloff forced more bullish bets to close. By the afternoon, it traded near $65,500, leaving leveraged traders at risk of losing their positions before any rebound.
By Saturday evening, CryptoSlate data showed Bitcoin near the bottom of its rolling 24-hour range of $63,278 to $69,052 after finally losing $64,000.
CryptoSlate's Bitcoin price page puts the asset down 6.5% over 24 hours, 15.8% over seven days and 19.7% over 30 days. It recorded $31.59 billion in trailing 24-hour trading volume.
Leveraged longs face forced reductions
Newhedge's futures dashboard recorded a $919,774 Binance BTCUSDT long-liquidation event at $65,976 at 14:26 UTC on Nov. 14. It recorded another worth $781,412 at $65,892 at 14:39 UTC.
At 14:48 UTC, Newhedge recorded a $260,381 Bybit BTCUSDT long liquidation at $65,571. These are individual forced closures of bullish bets, not a market-wide liquidation total or the traders' net losses.
Unlike simply holding Bitcoin, a leveraged long can be reduced or closed when a falling price erodes the collateral supporting it. A later rebound does not reopen a liquidated position.
A futures position can be liquidated when the available collateral falls below the maintenance margin required to keep it open. The system initially attempts to reduce the deficit by offloading a position into the market using an Immediate or Cancel order.
Forced closures can add selling pressure as prices fall. The records do not establish what started Saturday's selloff or how much of the decline liquidations caused.
Even a recovery to $66,000 would leave Bitcoin below the roughly $69,225 close to the week. For leveraged bulls, the immediate challenge is keeping their positions open long enough to benefit from any recovery.

articles.title: Microsoft 365 Outage Resolved, Cyberattack Ruled Out
articles.text:
Microsoft confirms global outage resolved, rules out cyberattack
Microsoft attributed the outage to a network capacity upgrade issue, confirming that the disruption was unrelated to cyberattacks or AI agents.
Microsoft said it restored Microsoft 365 services after a global outage disrupted Outlook, Teams and other applications for more than 24 hours, reiterating that the disruption was not caused by a cyberattack.
On Saturday, the company said it “restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions,” directing customers to incident MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center.
On Friday, Microsoft said that the outage stemmed from a problem introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade that emerged after a recent network change. “This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents,” the company said.
The company said it addressed the underlying issue and restored services gradually, checking stability before proceeding to the next stage. Microsoft apologized for the disruption and said it would publish a full post-incident report once its review is complete.
The outage began Thursday, disrupting access to Exchange Online mailboxes and features linked to Outlook, Teams and Microsoft Copilot. Government agencies in Japan, Singapore and the United States experienced email problems, while connections between Microsoft 365 and AI assistants were also affected.
OpenAI said the Microsoft 365 connector in ChatGPT was operating normally again, while Anthropic also marked its Microsoft 365 connector and Claude for Outlook incident as resolved.
Related: Coinbase restores trading after AWS outage disrupts markets

articles.title: Peter Schiff argues Bitcoin may fall below $16,500 by year-end if $50,000 breaks next
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Schiff said a $50,000 break could send Bitcoin below $16,500 before year-end, extending his earlier downside warnings.
- CryptoSlate’s Nov. 14 afternoon observations showed Bitcoin at $65,850 and Ethereum at $1,851, above Schiff’s stated triggers.
- Strategy’s Nov. 9 filing reported 850,364 BTC and about $5 billion in its USD Reserve, supplying dated context for Schiff’s conditional warning.
Bitcoin critic and gold advocate Peter Schiff said on Nov. 14 that a Bitcoin break below $50,000 could send it toward a level below $16,500 before the end of 2026. The call extends his earlier downside warnings, while Bitcoin traded near $65,850 on Saturday afternoon.
In his 05:53 GMT post, @PeterSchiff said a break of $50,000 could lead to “a quick trip to the 2022 low below $16.5K.” He said a retest before year-end would not surprise him.
According to CryptoSlate data at 15:02 GMT on Nov. 14, Bitcoin traded at $65,850, down 4.36% over 24 hours. It was 47.82% below its Oct. 6, 2025 all-time high of $126,198.
Peter Schiff extends his earlier Bitcoin calls
Schiff’s latest post gives a more specific downside marker than his earlier warnings. On Feb. 19, @PeterSchiff said a break below $50,000 would make a test of $20,000 “highly likely.” On June 2, he said the same break should be followed by a quick fall below $20,000.
The November call retains that $50,000 condition while explicitly naming a level below $16,500 and a timeframe before year-end. His June wording already allowed for prices below $20,000, so it should not be read as having established a precise floor there.
The $50,000 area also appeared in prior CryptoSlate reporting on Bitcoin’s risks. CryptoSlate’s July 1 analysis discussed a possible retest of $50,000-$55,000 amid ETF, policy and Strategy risks. That historical scenario is separate from Schiff’s new year-end call.
In a later Saturday post, @PeterSchiff argued that prospective buyers were already invested and that artificial intelligence had diverted attention from Bitcoin. He also alleged rising hacking risk and said the Trump-driven rally was over. Those were his explanations for expecting further weakness.
Peter Schiff attached a warning about Bitcoin-holding company Strategy to the forecast, saying a year-end retest would mean “curtains for $MSTR.” MSTR is Strategy’s listed common stock.
Strategy’s Nov. 9 filing reported holdings of 850,364 BTC as of Nov. 8, acquired for about $64 billion at an average cost of $75,456 per bitcoin, including fees and expenses. A lower Bitcoin price would reduce the market value of those holdings.
The filing also reported about $5 billion in its USD Reserve for preferred-stock dividends and debt interest, plus $146 million in USD Cash for broader treasury purposes. Those balances do not establish that a fall to Schiff’s target would force Strategy to sell Bitcoin or close.
Schiff’s criticism of Strategy predates Saturday’s post. CryptoSlate reported in March on his objections to its preferred-stock funding model.
In his 13:30 GMT post, @PeterSchiff also warned about Ethereum. He said a break of an uptrend around $1,600 could bring the next support level at what he described as the 2022 low just below $1,000.
Ethereum traded at $1,851 at 15:03 GMT, according to CryptoSlate data, down 4.95% over 24 hours. It was 62.64% below its Aug. 24, 2025 all-time high of $4,954, but remained above the $1,600 level Schiff identified. The year-end timeframe appeared in his Bitcoin post; his Ethereum post described chart levels without assigning that same timeframe.
The immediate price test in Schiff’s argument is still $50,000 for Bitcoin. In the afternoon CryptoSlate observations, both Bitcoin and Ethereum remained above the respective trigger levels he cited.

articles.title: MegaETH Parent Cuts 20% of Staff Amid AI Expansion
articles.text:
MegaETH parent cuts 20% of staff amid restructuring, AI push
MegaETH co-founder Shuyao Kong said the restructuring affected employees who helped build the project’s blockchain, wallet and ecosystem.
MEGA, the organization behind Ethereum layer-2 network MegaETH, has reduced its workforce by 20% following months of restructuring as it expands into artificial intelligence products.
On Friday, MegaETH co-founder Shuyao Kong said the organization had reorganized its teams, resulting in the departures of staff who worked on its blockchain, wallet, ecosystem support and communications. Kong did not disclose the number of employees affected or when the layoffs occurred. She said MEGA’s founders, early employees and core engineering team remain committed to the organization.
“We’ve brought together new capabilities and reorganized our teams, a process that has resulted in a 20% reduction in our staff,” Kong said. “These are people who helped build MEGA from its earliest days.”
The workforce reduction comes as MEGA shifts its focus toward developing products on the MegaETH network, including artificial intelligence services. The organization has committed $30 million to the initiative, although Kong did not directly link the layoffs to its new strategy.
In a whitepaper, MegaETH co-founders Yilong Li and Lei Yang outlined a proposed inference market aimed at giving users access to competing AI service providers. Their approach seeks to address concerns about whether providers use the advertised models and how they handle customer data.
Kong said MEGA plans to launch a public inference market in December.
Related: MegaETH mainnet to launch Feb. 9 after clocking 35K TPS in testing

articles.title: Crypto's $168 million election: 78 winners, 13 newcomers and one costly defeat
articles.text:
Quick Take
- CryptoSlate tracked $168 million in outside spending by five crypto-focused super PACs.
- Explore 78 supported winners by congressional experience, party, incoming seat, and spending received.
- The roster includes established crypto bill sponsors, first-time entrants, and lawmakers with unresolved policy disagreements.
Crypto super PACs backed 78 candidates who have won seats in Congress. Just 13 of them will enter Congress for the first time. Most of the winning roster already has a record in Washington. It includes the author of the House's crypto market-regulation bill, five representatives moving to the Senate, and a senator who supported stablecoin legislation but helped stop the broader market bill from advancing.
The newcomers could change the direction of districts whose earlier representatives opposed those measures.
CryptoSlate's review follows $168 million in reported outside spending by five crypto-focused super PACs across the 2025-2026 election cycle. The total includes support for unsuccessful candidates and attacks on opponents.
Ohio alone absorbed $64 million in an effort to elect Jon Husted and defeat Sherrod Brown. Brown won. Those results leave the industry with experienced advocates and prospective allies, alongside expensive defeats and unresolved disagreements.
Understanding what it gained requires looking at the people behind the tally and the decisions they will face on exchanges, stablecoins, and taxes.
Most crypto-backed winners already know Congress
Of the 78 winners, 57 are returning to the same chamber, five are moving from the House to the Senate, and three are former members coming back. The 13 first-time entrants make up about one-sixth of the group. Much of the industry's successful electoral activity therefore preserved legislators with existing experience and positions.
| Congressional status | Supported winners | 
|---|---|
| Returning to the same chamber | 57 | 
| Moving from the House to the Senate | 5 | 
| Former members returning | 3 | 
| Entering Congress for the first time | 13 | 
The spending also reached most of these candidates well before November. Fifty received no supportive general-election spending from the five committees: 47 were backed only in 2026 primaries or runoffs, and three only in 2025 special elections.
Every first-time entrant received their support during a primary or runoff. These payments bought advertising and other election communications.
Under the Federal Election Commission's definition, independent expenditures advocate a candidate's election or defeat without coordination with the campaign or party. They are outside spending, rather than donations handed to candidates.
Backing someone in a primary can help determine which member of a party reaches the general election. That gives the committees an opportunity to influence the choices available in November, even when they spend nothing supporting the eventual nominee afterward.
Meet the newcomers
Adrian Boafo and Jasmine Clark received the most support among the 13 first-time entrants: $5 million and $4 million, respectively, all from Protect Progress during their primaries. Together, they accounted for 67% of the $14 million spent supporting this newcomer group.
Their districts also offer a concrete way to assess what might change. Steny Hoyer, whom Boafo succeeds in Maryland's 5th District, voted against both the House's CLARITY market-structure bill and the GENIUS stablecoin bill in July 2025.
David Scott, who long represented Clark's Georgia district, voted against both as well. Boafo arrives with state legislation behind him. He sponsored Maryland's blockchain and digital-currency task force, established by a law approved in May. Its assignment is to study the technology's use and regulation, with recommendations due in October 2027.
He also sponsored a separate staking-services bill addressing restrictions and a securities exemption for qualifying services. The retrieved record shows a hearing, rather than enactment. His record gives the industry a reason to engage him on federal rules.
Clark's documented campaign commitments take a different form. Stand With Crypto's summary of her December 2025 questionnaire describes support for holding crypto in a personal wallet and for broad stablecoin availability.
The comparison with Scott requires one qualification: Everton Blair filled Scott's unexpired term after his death and is Clark's immediate predecessor. Scott's 2025 votes establish the district's earlier record on the two bills. They do not establish Blair's position or guarantee that Clark will vote differently on whatever text comes next. Both Boafo and Clark could change how their districts approach crypto legislation.
Ohio's $64 million defeat
The largest spending effort in the review ended with the committees' preferred candidate losing. Defend American Jobs and Digital Freedom Fund reported $40 million supporting Husted and $24 million opposing Brown in Ohio's Senate election. Brown won.
The combined $64 million accounted for about 38% of the five-PAC total. It was almost as much as the approximately $64 million spent supporting all 78 eventual winners.

Ohio combines support for Jon Husted and opposition to Sherrod Brown. The winners slice is support only across all stages. Other spending includes all remaining activity and classification conflicts. The slices do not overlap. CryptoSlate reconciled periodic reports through Oct. 14 with later notices and amendments. Provisional figures include estimates/unpaid notices; transfers and a separate $13,308 unpaid memo are excluded.
- Ohio: Husted support + Brown oppositionUSD 64.05M38.1%
- Support for all 78 winnersUSD 64.44M38.3%
- All other reviewed spendingUSD 39.64M23.6%
The Ohio figure combines support and opposition spending; the winners figure includes support only. Both come from the reconciled five-PAC ledger for the same cycle and cutoff.
The Ohio effort puts the long winners list in perspective: one defeat accounted for an extraordinary share of the money. Brown was also one of seven candidates who won despite opposition spending from these committees.
The incoming Congress will include lawmakers the industry supported and others it spent heavily trying to defeat.
The party split changes in the Senate
The winners divide evenly between the parties: 39 Democrats and 39 Republicans.
Their distribution across the chambers is much less balanced. Seven of the eight Senate winners are Republicans, with Virginia's Mark Warner the only Democrat in that group.

Opposition-only beneficiaries and unresolved races are excluded. This is not the party balance of the full chamber, and spending does not establish its effect on the result.

Each person is counted once, including recipients of multiple PACs’ support. Snapshot: Nov. 10, 2026, 08:37 UTC; certification unverified. Opposition-only beneficiaries and unresolved races are excluded. This is not the party balance of the full chamber, and spending does not establish its effect on the result.
- Democrats1 winners12.5%
- Republicans7 winners87.5%
Democrats' victory in both chambers changes who will control committees and bring legislation forward. The overall bipartisan tally conceals how heavily the supported Senate roster leans toward the incoming minority.
This is a selected group of election winners, not a count of everyone who favors crypto legislation. CryptoSlate's earlier report on 241 winners rated favorably by Stand With Crypto used the advocacy group's assessments, a different measure from documented spending by these five PACs.
Neither tally includes every senator who will serve next year, since many were not up for election.
Three allies, three different roles
French Hill's reelection preserves an author of legislation the industry wants passed. The Arkansas Republican sponsored the House CLARITY Act, which would divide oversight of digital-asset markets between the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.
He voted for that bill and GENIUS in July 2025, while Defend American Jobs and Fairshake reported a combined $1 million supporting him across the primary and general election.
Hill helped move CLARITY through the House on a 294–134 vote. He returns with that experience, although Democratic control will change the leadership of the Financial Services Committee he currently chairs. His next role and the compromises he will support remain to be determined.
Andy Barr brings a similar House voting record into a different chamber. The Kentucky Republican won a Senate seat after $8 million in supportive primary spending from Defend American Jobs and Fellowship. He voted for both House bills and chaired the Financial Institutions subcommittee in the outgoing Congress. His move gives the Senate a lawmaker who has already voted for a crypto market framework.
Warner demonstrates how far positions can diverge within the industry's own winners list. Fellowship reported $150,000 supporting his primary campaign. He voted for GENIUS in June 2025, then voted against advancing CLARITY in September 2026. In his explanation of that vote, Warner said the proposal lacked adequate restrictions on the president and senior officials profiting from crypto. He supported a federal regulatory framework while withholding support from legislation he considered deficient on ethics.
The September 15 vote was on cloture on the motion to proceed, a procedural step toward considering the bill. It failed 49–50. Warner's vote therefore records opposition to advancing that proposal at that stage, rather than rejection of every possible market-regulation bill. His position gives the industry a specific negotiating problem.
Agreement on stablecoins and a broader desire for federal rules can coexist with a demand for restrictions the bill's supporters have not accepted. Winning his seat again does nothing by itself to resolve that disagreement.
What changes for crypto users
The legislation these lawmakers write, amend, and oversee could affect how an exchange handles your assets, how you redeem a stablecoin, and what you must calculate when filing taxes. Each area is at a different stage.
Exchange rules remain a legislative negotiation. The House CLARITY proposal would establish a federal framework for digital-commodity trading, including registration and customer-protection obligations.
The allocation of authority between regulators determines which rules a platform must follow and who enforces them. Hill has helped write that framework, Barr has voted for its House version, and Warner has identified conditions for advancing it in the Senate.
If the current Congress leaves the bill unfinished, it will need to be reintroduced in the next one. The election preserves experienced participants in that work, while leaving the actual agreement unresolved.
Stablecoin safeguards are moving into implementation. GENIUS became law in July 2025. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency finalized its implementing rule in October, with the law and that rule due to take effect on January 18, 2027.
Its reserve and redemption requirements concern the assets backing stablecoins and the process for getting dollars back. Other regulatory work continues: the Federal Reserve's September package contains proposals. Returning lawmakers will oversee implementation and may seek changes to the statute, so a vote for GENIUS does not settle every subsequent decision about issuers and their customers.
Tax relief has a supported lawmaker behind it, but remains a proposal. Steven Horsford received $1 million in general-election support from Fairshake and voted for both House crypto bills. The Nevada Democrat also joined the original sponsors of a digital-asset tax package that advanced through Ways and Means by 38–5 in September.
The introduced text of H.R.10357 includes simplified treatment of qualifying dollar stablecoins and a gain-and-loss exclusion for digital assets used to pay eligible network or transaction fees totaling $10 or less per underlying transaction. Someone paying such a fee with a token can currently have a disposal to account for, requiring its acquisition cost and value when spent. The proposal aims to remove that calculation for qualifying fees, rather than create a general exemption for small crypto purchases.
The package also pairs simpler accounting options with restrictions on claiming losses after selling and rapidly repurchasing substantially identical assets. The committee advanced a substitute, and the measure has not become law. Existing IRS obligations continue to apply.
Crypto's winning roster preserves lawmakers who have written bills and adds candidates with positions voters can now follow in office. Its political influence will become more tangible when those people decide which customer protections, tax provisions, and limits on officials' financial interests they are willing to put into law.
