- The Ring Drone Cam. A drone that can go inspect and see anything in your house: useful! Also terrifying dystopia hellscape! I am desperately curious to know everything about how this $250 gizmo works — though I can tell you confidently my wife will never allow it in our house.
A lot of you out there in the Installerverse have become iPhone Duo users over the last few weeks, and I’ve heard a lot about how you’re all using Apple’s new foldable phone. (I’d say the sentiment in my inbox is roughly 80 percent positive, 5 percent negative, 15 percent deeply confused about interface choices.) I’ve also gotten some questions about which Duo apps are great, and how best to set yours up.
Alas, I do not have a Duo. So I turned to The Verge’s Allison Johnson, who coauthored our review of the device and has used it as aggressively as anyone I know. I asked her to share how she’s wielding the Duo, and she sent over a truly unhinged color scheme and otherwise a bunch of very good ideas. Her’s her homescreen, plus some info on the apps she uses and why:
The phone: iPhone Duo.
The wallpaper: It’s one of those color gradient options you can pick in iOS. I was trying to go for a minimalist thing.
The apps: NYT Games, Kindle, Headspace, Spotify, Google Maps, Safari, Messages, Mail.
So I tried the whole aspirational “dress for the homescreen you want” thing for a few days, with just a few apps like Headspace and NYT Games, and it was a miserable failure. It just made me mad every time I had to search for Messages. I added a row of essential apps to the bottom of the screen and a big calendar widget, and things have been much better.
There’s a big widget / shortcut to TypeDraw, which is a fantastic app on the Duo that makes the whole phone behave like a physical notebook. It’s great with the Apple Pencil. I also realized I need weather close by, so I added a giant widget to the left panel of the homescreen.
I also have a shortcut for the built-in lo-fi playlists on iOS, which is handy if I need to pop in earbuds and play something instrumental so I can focus real quick. Highly recommended to anyone who hasn’t discovered these yet and also gets overstimulated! They’re already on your phone!
I did nuke the dock entirely in my minimalist experiment and I’m actually fine with it. Maybe I’ll never go back to the dock again.
I also asked Allison to share a few things she’s into right now. Here’s what she sent back:
- I don’t have a Switch 2 so I’m having extreme Zelda FOMO right now. I WISH I was playing Ocarina of Time but I’m just playing through every last bit of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 on my PS5 to distract myself.
- I’m like 20 minutes away from finishing Widow’s Bay and that has been a really fun watch.
- I just finished reading the Planet Money book, which is like, The Economy For Dummies. It’s pretty entertaining and was very helpful for an economy dummy like me.
- I also got a book called Coffee, For Here by an award-winning barista and creator named Morgan Eckroth. They have lots of specialty drink recipes you can make with a home espresso setup. I made one over the weekend and I’m still thinking about how good it was. The photos are beautiful too.
Crowdsourced
Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com or message me on Signal — @davidpierce.11 — with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week.
“Search, a browser developed by a small Parisian design studio of all things. I’d say they have created the classy European cousin of Arc, based on Webkit so it’s super light & responsive on Mac while also having the flexibility of Chrome extensions.” — Elliot
“Trying out Monarch to potentially break my years-long Quicken habit. So far I’m about 90% sure I’m switching.” — Bruce
“Dungeon Crawler Carl. I recently started listening to the audiobook. It has consumed my life. I listen to it on my drive to work, I take breaks at work to listen to it, I play it throughout my day, and eventually fall asleep listening to it. It’s almost 200 hours of content and Jeff Hays does an amazing job voicing all the characters. I’m currently on book seven of eight, and not looking forward to the withdrawals as we wait for book 9. Seriously, check it out.” — William
“Brenpoly on YouTube has open-sourced his “I built an Apple Vision Pro for $5” project. It’s a great watch even if you don’t dabble in 3D printing. It also shows how much potential there is for affordable VR with just the phones in our pockets and some very clever people and communities.” — Owen
“For anyone with an iPhone Duo. On the outer display, Safari keeps a column down the side for its buttons, and web pages stop short of it. I’m a Duo owner, and am now using a great Safari extension called Widen that runs pages underneath that column: ~25% more page, with text kept clear of the buttons.” — Marcus
“I took my kid to see Wildwood, the new Laika movie, this past weekend and left the theater with my jaw on the floor and dragging a few feet behind me. It is extraordinary. For me, put it up there with the all time Studio Ghibli greats. (I know, I know, but I’m serious.) In a way that no Marvel movie special effects have done, I sat at multiple times in the movie thinking, ‘I just can’t believe humans made this.’” — Stephen
“I am a browser snob, constantly flitting back and forth trying to find the one that combines speed with features with proper UX with privacy. I had begrudgingly settled on Safari for Apple and Chrome for everything else when I stumbled upon Brave Origin. It’s a little steep at a one-time purchase of $59, but it’s completely cross platform, syncs, and gets rid of all the Brave cruft. It’s just a good, minimal, fast Chromium-based browser.” — Kait
“Queen’s Domain, a wonderful King’s Field-like game, was released this past weekend and it conjures up all those familiar FromSoftware feelings of combat and exploration! Highly recommended, it’s quite the experience.” — Kyle
“I finished Jet Lag: The Game’s Japanorama, and it is the absolute best tourism video series for Japan without trying at all to be one. It is part scavenger hunt, part race across Japan, and shows off the wonderful scenery and the beautiful public transit of the country. I learnt that Japan loves making lists (OCD folks rejoice!) and has lists of Three Views, Three Great Gardens, 100 Best Sunsets, 100 Remarkable Waters and many more.” — Utkarsh
Signing off
I’m working on a story about the new era of hardware hacking, in which people are suddenly discovering they can vibe-code their way to a better TV, the e-reader of their dreams, and a million other things besides. In almost all my conversations, one thing keeps coming up: the M5Stack developer kits. This company will send you an ESP32-based device you can hack to bits, whether you’re looking for something with an E Ink display or something with a round touchscreen. I’m about to spend an alarming amount of money buying these things, and an equally alarming amount of time making Claude Code do weird stuff with them. I’m already stealing ideas from the fabulous M5Stack subreddit. If you get up to something fun while hardware hacking this weekend, tell me all about it.
See you next week!

articles.title: Uber drivers' information stolen in a third-party hack - Engadget
articles.text:
Uber drivers' information stolen in a third-party hack
An AI provider working with Uber was hacked in October.
Uber has revealed in a filing with several attorneys general that the personal information and licenses of thousands of its drivers were compromised in a data breach. In the filing, which shows the notices it sent its drivers about the breach, Uber said that one of its service providers had been hacked on October 9. The attackers stole internal credentials, which they then used to access Uber's data connected to that provider.
The company told TechCrunch that the third-party vendor involved in the incident was Fireworks.ai, a cloud platform that gives its clients access to open-source AI models. Fireworks admitted that it suffered a data breach last month and that the incident had compromised its clients' data. It attributed the hack to attackers that belong to a cybercriminal group, which sells stolen tokens used to access large language models. It's unclear if the stolen information was also sold or leaked online.
Neither company has revealed how many drivers were affected. According to TechCrunch, though, the driver's licenses of 3,430 people from South Carolina, 2,567 in Massachusetts and 1,873 in Rhode Island were exposed in the incident.

articles.title: Jensen Huang and the decline of the visionary showman founder CEO
articles.text:
On January 6th, 2025, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang got his rockstar moment at last. He strode triumphantly onstage, hand raised in the air, to the claps and cheers of a 14,000-person arena absolutely packed with influencers and fans, their faces awash in blue glow, as he made his entrance in a black leather jacket that shimmered in the stadium’s lights.
Jensen Huang and the decline of the visionary showman founder CEO
The Steve Jobs of GPUs has been shown the door.
Few are cheering for Jensen Huang now. He has left Nvidia after seemingly enabling two chip smuggling scandals and allegedly having three extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy at the same time he was mingling with President Donald Trump.
The world is watching to see if this scandal might disrupt the entire US AI industry and perhaps destabilize the stock market along with it. That’s because Huang wasn’t merely running the first $5 trillion company, he was the visionary leader in control of the must-have GPUs powering the worldwide AI boom, part of a company that represents around 6 percent of the S&P 500 stock market index all by itself. And he didn’t plan for succession if he ever stepped down.
The 63-year-old once said he preferred to die on the job; he once suggested he’d work until he was 90 or 100, then carry on leading the company as a robot.
It’s not easy to replace Huang, partly because he had no deputies. Around 60 employees reported directly to the CEO. “He built the company around himself, and everything that happened there flowed through him,” says IDC analyst and former computing journalist Tom Mainelli.
“Jensen is Nvidia, and Nvidia is Jensen,” Jon Peddie, a computer industry analyst who’s been tracking Nvidia since its inception, tells me.
But Nvidia isn’t Jensen anymore. He has left the company he cofounded 33 years ago. It’s the end of an era, and not just for Nvidia — because Jensen Huang was Big Tech’s last true example of a visionary showman founder CEO.
“He was both the visionary and the tactical leader, the closest thing tech has had to Steve Jobs,” Moor Insights & Strategy chief analyst Pat Moorhead tells me.
Elon Musk didn’t exactly found Tesla and has quite the track record of broken promises, and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg has proven to be neither visionary nor showman so far. Google’s Larry Page and Sergey Brin stepped away in 2019 as their company dealt with growing employee turmoil, leaving the company in the hands of Sundar Pichai, and both Microsoft and Apple have each passed the torch twice since the days of Bill Gates and Steve Jobs.
Some say Apple’s Steve Jobs broke the CEO mold, but he created a mold of his own. Huang was one of countless tech leaders who followed his example by introducing their products in keynote speeches, adopting a single recognizable piece of clothing like Jobs’ trademark black turtleneck, and even occasionally teasing “one more thing” for the surprise at the end of their presentations. In the newsroom, we’d sometimes joke about the Jobs wannabes; many were stiff suits who didn’t have the credibility to pull it off.
I thought Huang might be a Jobs wannabe, too, the first time I saw that he’d adopted a black jacket as his uniform. (It was not always a leather jacket; an earlier version was a Nvidia-branded softshell.) Huang later insisted on wearing a jacket even when the temperature was hot — more than once, I saw him sweat profusely rather than take it off. Unlike Jobs, he also held quite a few keynotes when he didn’t have much news to share; he liked to repeat the company’s previous accomplishments as if they were brand-new.
But even if Huang didn’t have the same gravitas as Jobs, he did have exciting tech up his sleeves and loved to demo it onstage. He knew how to get people excited about the future of visual computing with eye-opening gaming graphics, physics and lighting demos, and eventually image recognition, AI weather simulations, digital copies of real-world factories, and the robots that can virtually train in them.
His Nvidia tried to educate people about the how and why of GPUs, too; I still remember in 2008 when Nvidia invited the Mythbusters to demo the difference between serial processing and parallel processing by firing a 1,100-nozzle paintball gun to “paint” the Mona Lisa in one shot.
What I didn’t know back then: Huang was a visionary founder. He took Nvidia to fame and fortune through a series of tremendous bets.
In 1996, three years after he cofounded the company at a Denny’s diner, Nvidia nearly went out of business while working on a failed graphics chip for the Sega Dreamcast game console. But even though he didn’t deliver that chip, Huang personally convinced Sega to invest $5 million afterward, The Wall Street Journal reported in 2024.
He then turned around and bet the company again on the Riva 128 PC graphics accelerator, an effort so ambitious he had to lay off over half of Nvidia’s roughly 100 staffers, skip the prototyping stage, and rush it straight to production, and he still only had one month of payroll left by the time it shipped, The New Yorker wrote in 2023. Thankfully, it was a success, selling a million units in just four months and paving the way for both the GeForce GPU and a long-term relationship with chip fabricator TSMC.
Roughly eight years later, Huang decided it wasn’t enough to be the leader in PC gaming graphics alone. He bet the company’s entire gross profit, he told podcaster Lex Fridman, on shipping a new feature inside those graphics cards that no one had asked for: CUDA. It was the ability to use a GPU for other kinds of computing tasks beyond graphics, and Huang said it increased the cost of every GeForce graphics card by 50 percent.
“Originally there was no market or market demand for it. It was almost as if they built it because they could,” says Peddie. “Jensen had the vision for what it could be and the courage to pursue it in spite of the opinions of others.”
“NVIDIA was effectively investing in a computing platform that extended far beyond graphics, with no guarantee of a near-term return,” says HotTech analyst Dave Altavilla.
“Huang saw that a GPU was really a parallel computer that happened to render graphics. CUDA turned that insight into a platform, and it’s why NVIDIA was ready when AI arrived,” Mainelli tells me.
It was a bad time for graphics cards to suddenly cost more. When the Great Recession hit in 2007–2009, and Nvidia laptop graphics chips also started failing due to design defects, the company lost 80 percent of its market value.
But Huang believed in CUDA enough to invest even more. “He literally handed out high-end NVIDIA GPUs to researchers at industry conferences, while the company seeded universities like Stanford with hardware to encourage development on its platform,” says Altavilla. And by 2012, Nvidia’s potential for AI had started to emerge.
That’s when University of Toronto researchers used Nvidia GPUs to train a prize-winning image-recognition neural network called AlexNet, which is widely credited for sparking the AI revolution.
Not all of Huang’s visions panned out the way he publicly expected. That AlexNet demo directly led to Huang’s bets on chips for self-driving cars, he said, but he didn’t exactly predict AI — CUDA was instead thought of as better and more affordable supercomputing for researchers and scientists. In 2013, I also wrote about how his grand plan for the future of the company relied heavily on putting Nvidia chips in your phone, which didn’t pan out.
But that bet on ARM-based phone chips did put Nvidia inside every Nintendo Switch and may have helped make future “AI superchips” possible — the latest Nvidia AI server chips have ARM CPU cores. And in 2022, the leaders of the AI revolution launched the most groundbreaking AI tech yet on Nvidia hardware: ChatGPT. Six years earlier, Huang hand-delivered Nvidia’s first purpose-built AI workstation to OpenAI, and by 2022 Microsoft had strung together tens of thousands of Nvidia A100 GPUs to handle the load.
“Every time competitors got close, he moved the fight up a level: the chip, then the server, then networking with the $6.9 billion Mellanox deal, then the full rack, all tied together by CUDA,” says Moorhead. “The speed came from how he ran the company,” he adds. “Decisions that took other companies four weeks took Nvidia four days.”
“Decisions that took other companies four weeks took Nvidia four days.”
As Nvidia’s fortunes and profit ballooned — thousands of dollars in pure profit every single second! — and as it became clearer that AI would reshape the world in one way or another, something strange happened. Huang became a celebrity. In summer 2024, The Wall Street Journal and social media chronicled that he received a hero’s welcome in his birthplace of Taiwan. He stopped over and over to sign autographs, including one on a woman’s chest.
In person, at presentations, and in the company’s investor Q&As, I saw the tone shift. People began treating the leather-jacketed man like an actual rockstar instead of a wannabe rockstar, asking for photos and autographs and complimenting him rather than asking tough questions.
It felt like he’d attained Steve Jobs’ infamous “reality distortion field” at last — until he popped that bubble himself with his infidelity.
But one fewer reality distortion field in the world isn’t necessarily a bad thing, and as Apple has shown, a company doesn’t go bust just because its charismatic founder is gone. Tim Cook made Apple the most profitable company in the world. The question now is: who for Nvidia?
“He was the king,” says Peddie. “Make no mistake – it was the Jensen Huang company. He called all the shots, took all the glory, and shouldered all the blame.”
Does Nvidia work without Huang?
Even without a named successor, analysts don’t think Nvidia is in big trouble yet.
“This is a stock shock, not a business shock, for the next year. The roadmap and manufacturing are locked in through 2027,” says Pat Moorhead, Moor Insights & Strategy. “The question is whether Nvidia keeps inventing at Jensen’s pace once those plans run out. The bigger risk than any rival chip is customers hedging during a vacuum. That is why the next CEO needs technical credibility, an operating model that doesn’t depend on one person, and a plan to protect CUDA.”
“Founder visionary, culture setter, leader, AI industry spokesperson etc., is the real loss. We don’t think anything changes strategically,” says Creative Strategies analyst Ben Bajarin.” The product roadmap is set and remains strong, and the next several generations are already in design, in tape-out or on order. NVIDIA is still the company best placed to ship its roadmap at scale, because it has spent years locking up the supply chain behind it, from leading-edge wafers and CoWoS-class packaging to HBM and the rack-level partners. That supply position does not walk out the door with one person.”
“He was the consummate showman, salesman, and visionary for NVIDIA, so he will be hard to replace,” says IDC analyst Tom Mainelli. “But the company’s technology road map is sound, and the team behind him is still there. Choosing the right person to replace him will be key, and there will undoubtedly be bumps along the way. But the company will survive.”
“Jensen built an exceptionally talented organization with a deep engineering bench, a mature, heavily-resourced software ecosystem, and strong customer relationships,” says Dave Altavilla, HotTech Vision and Analysis. “His departure undoubtedly leaves a leadership and strategic vision gap, but the technology, talent, and execution capabilities he helped establish aren’t going away. The real question is whether his successor can sustain that same long-term vision and willingness to invest ahead of the market.”
“No one in the company really wants to step into his shoes, so an outsider is going to have to be found,” says Jon Peddie of Jon Peddie Research. “Whoever that is will not be Jensen, won’t have the same ambitions, the same contacts and relationships, the same vision, or the same courage to make big, long-term bets. We’ve seen this in Apple, AMD, Intel, and other companies. So the stock will probably get battered around a bit until investors see some stability and fewer ‘what if’ questions.”

articles.title: Your new tech is still stuck in the year 1970 — here's why - Engadget
articles.text:
Your new tech is still stuck in the year 1970 — here's why
Don’t worry; your computer isn’t being transported back to the past.
There's a good chance you've seen the date January 1, 1970 on a computer or other device, even if you weren't alive back then. You might assume this represents a significant date in computing, or that it's a random placeholder date for when a machine fails to read the time. In actuality, while the date is not special in itself, it represents an important part of how computers keep time.
Like everything in computing, the method that leads to this date is finite, meaning we'll have problems with it in the future. This all ties into a more interesting discussion of how computers (and humans) keep track of time, which is more complicated than you might think.
The meaning of January 1, 1970
January 1, 1970 at 00:00 (midnight) UTC is the epoch of Unix time. An epoch refers to a specific, impactful moment, usually corresponding to the start of a timekeeping system. Unix was one of the first operating systems we would consider modern, beginning development in the late 1960s. It's the basis for many other operating systems that are known as "Unix-like," including Linux, macOS and Android. Windows is the main outlier.
When Unix was in development, its developers needed a way to keep track of time. A few early attempts used the system clock speed of 60Hz, but storing this in a 32-bit integer resulted in a value that would run out of room after less than 2.5 years. After some time, they changed the time-keeping to use seconds and chose January 1, 1970 as a "round" arbitrary date to begin at, figuring that the 32-bit integer for time wouldn't run out of space anytime soon (more on that later).
To this day, Unix time is kept by tracking the number of seconds that have passed since Jan 1, 1970 at midnight UTC. UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) was an obvious choice since it's already the standard for keeping track of time across time zones. It's simple for a computer to compare two numbers and calculate the difference between them without worrying about all the rules we have around time. The system converts the timestamp, including your time zone's offset from UTC, into our human-readable format.
You might see the 1970-01-01 date appear in spreadsheets, apps, file metadata, error screens and various other places. Unless this date happens to line up with someone's birthday or another major event, it's usually the result of an error. When a Unix-like system tries to check the time and runs into a problem or receives a 0 value, it will default to the epoch. If you live in a time zone that's behind UTC, you'll likely see these default values as late in the day on December 31, 1969 instead.
The year 2038 problem
Traditional Unix time is kept as a signed 32-bit integer, a binary value with 32 digits that can each be 1 or 0. Signed integers can track positive and negative numbers, while unsigned integers can only be positive. In the case of tracking time, using a signed value is necessary to track dates before 1970. Because the first (leftmost) bit of a signed integer is used to indicate whether it's negative, it cuts the range of possible values in half compared to an unsigned number.
An unsigned integer's maximum value is 2^31, or 4,294,967,295. A signed value can represent half of this in each direction, going as high as 2,147,483,647 and as low as -2,147,483,648. Unix time thus has an "expiration date." Once that upper limit of seconds has passed, the leftmost digit will become a 1, which causes the rest of the number to be interpreted as negative. This will happen on January 19, 2038 at 3:14:07 AM UTC, which is why you'll hear this called the "year 2038 problem." Once the integer overflows, the time will incorrectly show December 13, 1901 at 8:45:52 PM UTC and continue counting up from there.
Thankfully, we've had (and still have) plenty of time to implement workarounds before this date. Most modern Unix-like systems now use a 64-bit integer to keep track of time, which can keep track of seconds for some 292 billion years before overflowing — if anyone is still around by then, moving time to a 128-bit integer will be their problem. Your modern MacBook is 64-bit and will work fine, while a 32-bit device like an iPhone 4 will run into trouble.
The main risk for when 2038 rolls around is in old systems that can't easily be updated, like those embedded in appliances, vehicles, cameras and similar. Some of those won't be heavily affected even if they can't keep the exact time, but we'll have to replace any of those devices still around in 12 years if time is a critical factor.
Keeping track of time presents lots of challenges
You might wonder if this time problem is related to Y2K (which also had a similar name, "year 2000 problem"), which was a big worry going into the new millennium. While both revolve around computers keeping time, the past problem was caused by decimal shorthand, not binary overflow.
In the early days of computing, memory was extremely expensive, so programmers saved wherever possible. It was thus common to use two digits to indicate the year, assuming that the first two digits were always "19". Y2K was the worry that once the year hit 2000, computers would interpret "00" as 1900 (or another earlier date) instead of 2000, causing all kinds of problems for programs that relied on accurate time. It was a big scare at the time, but ended up not being nearly as terrible as expected (which, depending on who you ask, was either due to prevention efforts or because the issue was never huge to begin with).
Other time-tracking methods
Unix time is not the only way that computers handle the clock. Many machines have a real-time clock, which keeps track of the time similarly to a wall clock and retains power using the CMOS battery when the computer is powered off. When this battery dies, your computer's clock won't be right.
Windows, as the exception mentioned earlier, keeps track of time differences in 100-nanosecond ticks starting January 1, 1601 at midnight UTC. While it's much older than 1970, this epoch isn't random; the Gregorian calendar we use goes through a complete cycle every 400 years, so 1601 was the start of the most recent cycle at the time of Windows' development. It's an unsigned 64-bit integer value (as it's unlikely a computer would need to represent dates before 1601) that will become invalid on September 14, 30,828.
Finally, there's NTP (Network Time Protocol), which syncs your computer's time to extremely accurate time-keeping servers over the internet. If the computer's method of keeping the time ever fails or drifts, it receives corrections using NTP. There's a lot more to keeping track of time, like soon-to-be-retired leap seconds, daylight saving time, time zone changes, and calendar shifts, but now you understand more about what computers do to keep track of it.

articles.title: 'Root cause’ of nationwide ground stop is unknown, FAA says
articles.text:
The root cause of the longest halt in flight departures to U.S. airports since 9/11 remains unclear after a Saturday press conference by U.S. transportation officials.
Routers and networking equipment appeared to be involved in the technological disruption that grounded flights across the country, but a definitive cause has not been established as of Saturday afternoon.
The inability to pinpoint the reason for the infrastructure malfunctions led the Federal Aviation Administration to take actions that resulted in the grounding order, Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration, told reporters.
"Because of our lack of identifying the root cause, we were unwilling to take any risk that this propagation could actually result in a sensor losing connectivity with aircraft," he said.
"What we saw was instability. We couldn't explain the instability," Bedford added.
Officials reported issues with routers and networking equipment on Saturday, citing products and services from Cisco and L3Harris Technologies.
"Until I can build [the new architecture], I'm stuck with L3Harris, who owns this network," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said.
In a statement on X, L3Harris said that it, in partnership with other tech companies, has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber-optic system.
"We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," the statement said. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously."
On Friday, Duffy and Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin called for an air travel overhaul, with Duffy requesting $50 billion from Congress.
FAA administrator Bedford said that router updates were a matter of regular business for his agency and distinct from modernization allocations.
"We are constantly replacing 2,000, you know, Cisco 600 routers with Juniper routers, right? So this is ordinary course of business stuff. This is not part of the … FAA $12.5 billion modernization efforts. So let's not conflate those two things," Bedford said.

articles.title: $180 million Van Gogh tests the art market and collector confidence
articles.text:
A version of this article appeared in CNBC's Inside Wealth newsletter, a weekly guide to the high-net-worth investor and consumer. Sign up to receive future editions straight to your inbox.
The art auctions in New York next week could top $2 billion, as a treasure trove of masterpieces comes to the market for the first time in decades.
Total sales at Sotheby's, Christie's and Phillips are expected to be around $2.4 billion, which would equal last year's total, according to ArtTactic. Sotheby's alone is expected to pull in over $1.1 billion, with a single collection from The Blaquier-Arrieta Collection estimated at $450 million.
The collection includes the two big headliners of the week: Vincent van Gogh's landscape "Châtaigniers en fleurs," (Chestnut Trees in Flower) estimated at $180 million and Paul Cézanne's "Arlequin," estimated at $120 million. Neither has been seen in public for a half a century.
Sotheby's CEO Charles Stewart said demand is strong in the art market, especially for the highest quality blue-chip works, as rising stocks markets and private wealth boost the confidence of collectors.
"There's been enormous wealth creation and a lot of confidence in markets," Stewart said. "It's a global phenomenon. We're seeing recovery and greater interest across Asia and something really exciting happening from the Middle East across to Singapore and Europe and the U.S."
Christie's star of the week is Wassily Kandinsky's "Betonte Ecken," estimated at $60 million to $80 million. Christie's CEO Bonnie Brennan describes the market is "confident but discerning, rewarding truly exceptional works." She said recent gyrations in the stock market and fears of an AI bubble aren't likely to deter serious collectors.
"At the very highest end of our market, collectors tend to take a much longer-term view," Brennan said. "They understand that the opportunity to acquire a masterpiece may come only once in a generation, and that can be far more important than what the stock market has done in any particular week. In uncertain moments, the very best can actually become even more compelling."
The art market has continued to rebound this year after declines in 2023 and 2024, with auction sales in the first half up 70% over last year, to $6.8 billion, according to Bank of America.
Drew Watson, head of art services at Bank of America, said blue-chip art is outperforming, with Impressionist & Modern sales up 133% in the first half.
"Our outlook for the art market this November is cautiously optimistic," Watson said. "Improving liquidity, combined with an unusually strong concentration of fresh-to-market private collections, creates a favorable backdrop for the marquee sales."

articles.title: SpaceX catches upper stage of Starship rocket in historic first
articles.text:
After a booster explosion on Friday, SpaceX successfully caught the upper stage, or spacecraft, portion of its massive Starship rocket from orbit on Saturday — a triumphant milestone for the company.
SpaceX made the historic catch using its "chopsticks," mechanical arms attached to a launch tower, at its facility in Starbase, Texas.
Test Flight 15, the most ambitious Starship test yet, marked the first time Elon Musk's company attempted to catch both the rocket's booster and upper stage.
Musk posted a video on X inspecting the upper stage craft after completing the capture.
During the first phase of the test flight on Friday, SpaceX failed to catch and recover the booster, instead diverting it to an offshore splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico where it exploded before hitting the water.
The rocket's upper stage then continued into orbit and flew around the Earth 14 times before successfully landing on SpaceX's launch tower, nicknamed Mechazilla.
The Hawaii Department of Transportation issued a temporary pause on some West Coast flights Friday, due to debris risk from the flight. Separately, the FAA issued a rare, nationwide ground stop due to telecommunications system failures. (Both of those orders have since been lifted.)
Making Starship a reliable and fully reusable rocket is critical to SpaceX's ambitions. In the near term, the company needs Starship to send more satellites into orbit to expand its Starlink satellite internet service, which is currently the company's profit center.
SpaceX is also expected to use Starship to bring astronauts and cargo from lunar orbit to the Moon's surface and back for NASA. Musk also has a grand vision to use Starship to "colonize Mars" and "make humanity multi-planetary."
During Test Flight 15 on Friday, SpaceX released another 26 of its newest Starlink v3 satellites into orbit, growing its commercial satellite internet network.
The company's constellation already included over 11,000 satellites in low Earth orbit. One Starship rocket can carry up to 60 Starlink v3 satellites, the company has said.

articles.title: Nvidia's leadership crisis rattles the AI trade. Here's how we're adjusting our portfolio
articles.text: Wall Street faced a major test last week as Nvidia's stunning leadership shake-up dominated the headlines and brought more uncertainty to the AI trade. Despite the turbulence, the S & P 500 secured a weekly gain of 2.5%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq added 2.3%. Both indexes were up so much on Monday and Wednesday that declines on Tuesday, Thursday, and Friday were no match. In fact, both the S & P 500 and Nasdaq have made sizeable dents in the losses they suffered in the postelection market rout on Nov. 5. While Nvidia shares fell another 2% on Friday, the market ended the week under pressure for a different reason. It was the potential for multiple Federal Reserve rate hikes over the next few meetings that led to the selling. Before Friday's open, the October producer price index turned in its highest yearly reading in nearly four years. Headline PPI, a measure of wholesale inflation, was cooler than expected month over month. However, its year-over-year increase to 6.5% was all anyone cared about, especially after Tuesday's hot consumer inflation report . Here's a closer look at the three things that shaped our view of last week's market. Nvidia's C-suite shake-up Nvidia's leadership crisis sent shares tumbling nearly 13% for all of last week, bucking a broader rebound in semiconductor stocks. The Nvidia sell-off began Monday after reports that the chip giant's board was investigating CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China. The scandal escalated with reports that Huang had affairs with two Nvidia employees, culminating in his resignation Thursday. Longtime CFO Colette Kress was named interim CEO, a move that Jim Cramer was pleased with. While remaining confident in Nvidia's technology and management bench, Jim acknowledged the uncertainty surrounding its future . "A Jensen-less Nvidia is an Nvidia many will not want to own," he said Wednesday on " Mad Money ." We downgraded Nvidia to our hold-equivalent 2 rating Tuesday. While not looking to buy the dips, Jim said he was not abandoning the company either . Jim pointed to Apple's success after Steve Jobs and expressed confidence in Kress to right the ship. For longtime shareholders sitting on substantial gains, Jim emphasized capital preservation, urging investors to consider taking some profits rather than risk giving them back. He said Thursday: "If you are one of those millionaires, don't become a hundred-thousandaire." The next test for Nvidia will come when it reports earnings on Tuesday evening. Swapping Intel for AMD We're planning to exit our position in Intel and use the proceeds to initiate a position in rival Advanced Micro Devices once our trading restrictions allow. Jim said that Friday's decline in AMD is a " terrific opportunity " to buy the stock. The move reflects our growing confidence in AMD's ability to capitalize on booming demand for data center chips. Part of our thinking is that the turmoil at Nvidia could create opportunities for AMD to gain market share in graphics processing units (GPUs). We're also more confident in AMD's ability to meet growing demand for central processing units (CPUs), which are needed in data centers to run AI agents. The CPU story was one of the reasons we bought Intel earlier this year . AMD's advantage comes partly from its more flexible chip designs, allowing it to shift resources between personal computers and server processors more easily than Intel. That flexibility is particularly important as rising memory prices weigh on PC demand. Jim started saying he wanted to exit Intel and buy AMD on Wednesday. That's when we downgraded Intel to our sell-equivalent 3 rating and added AMD to our Bullpen watchlist. While painful, the planned swap means realizing a substantial loss on Intel. "Sometimes, you just have to admit you got it wrong," Jim said, reiterating his admission from the Investing Club's 4th Annual Meeting. Taking profits and diversifying We did make several trades last week to reduce our data center exposure, which allowed us to lock in gains and get bigger defensive stocks. On Monday, we trimmed our Eaton position despite its strong earnings, realizing a roughly 47% gain. The move reduces our exposure to the risk of hyperscalers scaling back spending as data center construction faces growing challenges. Eaton makes power management systems that are used to maximize energy efficiency. We also initiated a position in Constellation Brands . The maker of Modelo and Corona offers an inexpensive valuation, a nearly 3% dividend yield, and improving beer sales trends. We also see potential benefits from easing immigration policies. On Tuesday, we trimmed another 25 shares of Cardinal Health after its roughly 23% rally since the end of September, locking in a 24% gain. We remain confident in the healthcare distributor's long-term growth prospects. On Friday, we sold some shares of TJX Companies following a downgrade from Gordon Haskett, which raised concerns about competition from Ross Stores and lingering execution issues at its Marmaxx division. With earnings coming up Wednesday morning, we wanted to protect our gains, realizing an average profit of roughly 113%. We used the proceeds to buy more shares of Constellation Brands and Kimberly-Clark . Investors are underestimating Kimberly-Clark's ability to turn around Kenvue following its acquisition. Jim likes the combination of Kimberly-Clark's strong consumer products portfolio, which includes Huggies and Kleenex, and the household names of Kenvue, which include Tylenol and Band-Aid. (Jim Cramer's Charitable Trust is long NVDA, AAPL, INTC, ETN, STZ, CAH, TJX, KMB. See here for a full list of the stocks.) As a subscriber to the CNBC Investing Club with Jim Cramer, you will receive a trade alert before Jim makes a trade. Jim waits 45 minutes after sending a trade alert before buying or selling a stock in his charitable trust's portfolio. articles.title: Nvidia board urged to consider 'potential return of Jensen Huang' by two major investors
articles.text:
Two major Nvidia shareholders are calling on the board of directors to weigh all options for the company's future leadership, including "the potential return of Jensen Huang."
Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner posted a letter on X on Friday that urges Nvidia's board to "pursue a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding the future leadership of Nvidia." The letter is also signed by Atreides Management's Gavin Baker.
Nvidia was Altimeter Capital's largest disclosed equity holding in its most recent SEC filing, with a 9.4 million-share stake worth nearly $1.9 billion as of June 30. Atreides held 1.2 million shares worth nearly $250 million at the end of June.
The letter said Nvidia will be "capably led" by interim CEO Colette Kress, who served as Nvidia's CFO for 13 years before the board announced Thursday that she'd lead the company in Huang's absence.
"But the Founder and long time incredible leader of this extraordinary company has earned the right for a deliberate process that avoids any needless rush to replace him before all the facts are known," the letter concludes. The document did not call for Huang's immediate reinstatement.
Nvidia founder Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday amid multiple affair allegations, including one with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang, who also worked with Nvidia customer Megaspeed. The Singapore-based company is being investigated by the Justice Department for possibly redirecting some of its supply of Nvidia's restricted artificial intelligence chips to China.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on X Friday that he signed a petition asking to reinstate Huang. A petition circulating online called "Stand with Jensen" claims to have more than 100,000 signatures, including more than 5,000 current Nvidia employees.
Musk said on X Saturday that without Huang, some "critical deals will be lost."
Another letter sent Friday called on U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick to testify about Megaspeed before the House Intelligence Committee.
Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10 about whether the Commerce Department is "properly performing its broader role of preventing China from acquiring advanced AI chips," according to the letter. Huang has also been asked to testify.
The Commerce Department originally launched an investigation into Megaspeed that was moved to the Justice Department in 2025 after Nvidia's lawyer contacted a senior Commerce official, according to The New York Times.
President Donald Trump is scheduled to visit China on Thursday, but doesn't plan to raise Nvidia and the suspected spy affair during his meeting with Chinese president Xi Jinping, according to U.S. officials. Musk is expected to join Trump on the trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Nov. 18 and 19.

articles.title: How Nvidia turmoil and a Democratic Congress could reshape the AI trade, according to ETF experts
articles.text:
The largest technology stocks linked to the artificial intelligence trade could stand to benefit the most from Nvidia's woes and a Democratic-controlled Congress pushing back on data centers, according to investing experts interviewed on CNBC's "ETF Edge" earlier this week.
"We may have been put in an environment, as much as investors have sort of been looking for areas outside of Big Tech, where net-net Big Tech ends up as the winner once again," said Roundhill Investments CEO Dave Mazza, whose firm manages the Magnificent Seven ETF (MAGS).
Part of his bull case: Other players in the AI trade are positioned to fill Nvidia's chip demand if investors lose trust in the company after a tumultuous week that saw its iconic founder and CEO Jensen Huang resign.
"If we get into an environment where people can't trust … Nvidia, they're going to look for other sources for these chips because they need them," Mazza said during the "ETF Edge" interview, which occurred Monday as the Nvidia scandal grew but before Huang had resigned.
Discussing recent fund flow activity for the MAGS ETF, as well as for the Roundhill Neocloud ETF (NCLD) — which focuses on smaller market cap, specialized cloud computing companies — Mazza said, "In a weird way, [hyperscalers] may continue to benefit from this because they have the compute available. It's going to be more valuable if the demand is there."
The Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF ended the week in the green, albeit with a gain of less than 1%, while the Roundhill Neocloud ETF was up over 1%, though earnings from top holdings Coreweave and Nebius presented a mixed picture.
CoreWeave had its best day since April 2025 on Wednesday after its latest quarterly results, while Nebius shares sank after its Thursday report. The neocloud ETF remains deeply in the red since its August 2026 launch, down 39%, amid concerns about balance sheet strength, which could linger given Nvidia's role in financing the AI buildout. CoreWeave shares sank again on Friday, and Nvidia posted its longest losing streak since 2012 after its latest weekly losses.
Nvidia's interim CEO and current chief financial officer Colette Kress will have her first opportunity to reassure the market when Nvidia reports its third-quarter earnings next Tuesday. "Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders," Kress said in a statement issued on Thursday morning when the company announced Huang's exit.
Yorkville Ives partner and senior managing director Dan Ives said on "ETF Edge" on Monday that the market will remain optimistic about other AI chip players, like AMD and Alphabet, if Nvidia faces prolonged headwinds. Ives helped create the Dan IVES Wedbush AI Revolution ETF (IVES) while at Wedbush Securities, where he served as the managing director and global head of technology research before departing Wedbush to form his own firm earlier this year.
AMD finished trading this week up close to 13%, with Broadcom posting similar gains.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq index posted its best week since August as Nvidia's slump reshuffled the AI trade.
Yorkville Ives lowered its price target on Nvidia to $225 from $300 on Thursday after Huang's resignation, but maintained a buy rating on the stock, which finished the week at $162.85 per share.
"Nvidia remains the clear leader in GPU chips for the AI Revolution. They are roughly 2-3 years ahead of the nearest competitor and the demand trajectory the next few years is not changing because Jensen is gone," Ives wrote in a note to investors on Thursday. "The strategic roadmap is already essentially built around the next few family of chips and physical AI with 42k employees driving it. ... Valuation at roughly 10x 28 EPS is way too cheap once Nvidia gets through this storm and emerges on the other side."
The compute that does exist could become even more indispensable against the backdrop of a potential slowdown to the data-center buildout by Congress after the Democratic Party gains of Nov. 3 swept control of Congress, Mazza said.
Ives estimates that the "blue tidal wave" in Congress could mean 10% of planned data centers won't materialize on the low end, and 15%-20% on the high end, but he added that demand still outstrips supply four to one. "The compute is just that much more valuable in the capacity today than it was a week ago. So I could argue just more and more bullish, strong, get stronger," Ives said.
"The game is going to change for Big Tech. It will slow it down. But there's no overbuild, no bubble concerns. And I view that as actually a positive thing," he added.

articles.title: Rising rents draw Wall Street money to industrial outdoor storage lot investments across the U.S.
articles.text:
Nondescript lots holding idle bulldozers, trucks and other industrial equipment are a common sight in local real estate markets across the U.S., and increasingly, a focus for Wall Street private investment giants.
If you haven't noticed them, it's probably because they so easily fade into the landscape, just another non-branded bit of land in the miasma of suburbia. But Brookfield and Blackstone, two of the world's largest alternative asset managers, are among the institutional investors moving in on what the industry calls industrial outdoor storage, or IOS. Investors are eyeing these lots as the AI build-out increases the demand for heavy equipment.
"We have strong conviction in industrial outdoor storage, which plays a critical role in our supply chain," said Devin Barnwell, a managing partner and co-leader of Brookfield's logistics business.
He says that up until now, the segment has been fragmented, but Brookfield sees that changing.
"We see significant opportunity to bring institutional capital and operating expertise to this fragmented sector, improving the quality and efficiency of these assets while strengthening the resilience of our industrial supply chains," Barnwell said.
Brookfield spent $1.2 billion earlier this year to take Peakstone Realty Trust private, a deal completed in May that gave it a portfolio of more than 70 industrial properties, most of them outdoor storage yards.
Blackstone is also ramping up in the sector, mainly as a lender. Its real estate debt arm has made six loans to outdoor storage owners totaling more than $1.1 billion, including a $244 million loan in June to Alterra IOS to buy 37 properties.
Despite the billions being bet on the market by Wall Street, there is still opportunity in the market for individual investors and local entrepreneurs looking to park their money where others park their equipment.
"1,000 percent yes," said Adam Petrillo, an executive managing director at Newmark, a commercial real estate advisory firm, who co-leads its industrial outdoor storage practice.
Petrillo said smaller, non-institutional investors, still control a significant amount of well-placed storage in secondary markets. "The good news for smaller investors and mom and pops is that a good individual IOS site isn't necessarily 50 acres," Petrillo said.
Lots as small as three to five acres in primary or secondary markets can still yield a robust return, he said. "At that bite size, an individual can step in. We are not talking about tens of millions ... a three-acre, well-located IOS with multiple use cases can be found, marketed, leased, and stabilized," he added.
Hottest outdoor storage property markets
The numbers help explain the appetite.
Rents for industrial outdoor storage roughly doubled across eight major markets between 2020 and the third quarter of this year, according to data from Newmark Research and Alterra IOS, an owner of such properties. Average rent per usable acre rose 103.5%, to nearly $11,000 a month, compared with a 66% increase for traditional industrial space, such as indoor warehouses.
Rent growth, according to Alterra, is most closely tied to infrastructure and energy activity in the area, even more so than data center development specifically.
The value of these properties can also increase if located near a seaport, rail line, or highway. But the gains weren't uniform. Baltimore (204%), Houston (159%) and Norfolk (148%) led, while South Florida and Savannah IOS actually trailed traditional industrial.
Lisa DeNight, managing director, head of North American industrial research at Newmark, said that Savannah's IOS vacancy remains quite tight despite the rent figures. Recent port activity is a potential factor, according to Alterra. Savannah's container volumes more than doubled between 2010 and 2022 but have since declined, while Houston saw roughly 15% growth from 2022 to 2025.
Petrillo said that there is still plenty of room left for values to increase, so an investor jumping in now hasn't missed the game. "We are still in the very early innings," Petrillo said.
Sam Cheema co-founder of CanTex Capital, a Dallas-based firm that acquires overlooked industrial real estate in Texas, is seeing increased demand for these lots.
"It comes down to supply and demand," he said. "If you need a warehouse you can usually find one. Properly zoned infill IOS sites are much harder to find and every year more of them are converted to warehouses and other uses," he said, referencing multifamily housing units. The scarcity makes tenants sticky. "So a limited supply keeps shrinking. And because so much of the value is in the land itself, owners keep the option to redevelop the site as the area grows," Cheema added.
Because of the imbalance of supply and demand, rents and prices are rising across the board, according to Cheema, but no two IOS properties look alike, which has kept the door open for smaller investors.
"Big institutions want exposure to IOS, but ownership is fragmented across mom-and-pop owners and small businesses, so it's hard to deploy large amounts of capital without first aggregating these assets into portfolios," Cheema said.
Unlike traditional warehouses, there's no standard spec like square footage or clear height to compare them. "That lack of standardization along with the ongoing growth of the asset class, means there's still runway for small investors to find opportunities," Cheema said.
"Financing has improved as more lenders have a better understanding of IOS, but it's still largely local and regional banks," Cheema added.
Zoning is the biggest challenge.
"If you don't understand the city's plans for the area, you may end up owning a use they're trying to phase out," Cheema said.
CanTex Capital works with the city and neighborhoods before buying to ensure the impact aligns with the community's plan for its future.
Advantages over traditional industrial, multifamily real estate
Alex Sutterer, an executive vice president at NAI Hiffman, a Chicago-area commercial real estate firm, said that beyond being a place to store big equipment, IOS attracts investors for two main reasons: lower capital expenditure requirements than traditional industrial or multifamily properties and the potential for higher yields.
"Capital improvements are also less specific to individual tenants, so owners can direct spending toward the property's overall functionality," Sutterer said.
For private investors, IOS typically trades at a yield around one percentage point higher than traditional industrial properties, helping attract smaller investors and family offices. "We believe that gap will continue to narrow as more institutional capital enters this space," Sutterer added.
Even for industrial properties with similar yields, he said the credit profile of tenants is generally stronger for IOS.
Shallow-bay, multitenant industrial properties — industrial facilities that tend to be much smaller than big-box distribution warehouses — have comparable yields. But unlike the local businesses that tend to fill up shallow-bay sites, IOS tenants range from local businesses to those with investment-grade credit ratings, offering investors the potential for both yield and creditworthy tenants.
And institutional money is making IOS more competitive.
"Institutional capital has increased competition in IOS, and property values and lease rates have risen overall," Sutterer said.
He added smaller investors can still find opportunities below institutional deal-size thresholds, although that does not mean every smaller deal is priced fairly. "We see opportunities to add value and earn yield in deals below $3 million–$5 million," Sutterer said.
For local investors, that means there is the ability to build a portfolio at a smaller scale and hold the assets for cash flow, or aggregate more than $10 million in assets and seek a portfolio premium when selling to institutional capital.
But buyers need to understand what they are getting into. Due diligence on tenant demand by site and site function, and tenant turnover ratio, are important factors in buying the right asset. Market diversity can also provide protection, Sutterer said.
"In Chicago, no single user category accounts for more than 18% of IOS tenants, helping insulate the market from industry-specific slowdowns," he said. Tenants' tendency to stay and tight vacancy rates nationally are current advantages of the asset class. In Chicagoland, for example, vacancy is below 3%.
Still, all the due diligence in the world can't protect investors from some variables.
"No one outside the Federal Reserve can control the cost of debt," said Kellie McIvor, vice president of acquisitions at Redwood Living, an Ohio real estate development firm. She said that right now, the cost of debt for light industrial uses is lower than, say, for residential construction.
"However, interest rates are still high, with no relief in sight," McIvor said.
The Fed is expected to raise rates in December in its effort to tame inflation, and after this week's latest hot October CPI report, potentially hike twice more in early 2027, according to some Wall Street forecasts.
"Because lenders view them as riskier than a large institutional investor, smaller buyers can face more expensive debt and may be asked to bring more equity to the deal. That can make financing a small acquisition disproportionately expensive. ... More expensive debt means less room for error in execution," McIvor said.
A small buyer looking at a small site that requires no improvement may be able to fund the deal all on his own. "That's the dream! Own your business and the land it's on, outright!" she added.
Ross Blankenship, who owns two fenced contractor and fleet yards in Colorado's Vail Valley through Wins Parking, said the math has to work today. In a mountain market where little land is zoned for the use, he rents spaces for $210 a month for a car or pickup and $265 for a box truck or trailer, and charges $1,250 to $5,500 a month for contractor zones. Blankenship also runs Park Graph, the parking software he uses to rent the spaces.
The swing factor is vacancy, he said. "A full yard throws off more cash per dollar of capex than a small retail or office building. An empty one earns nothing," he said.
His advice for a first-time buyer: call 10 local contractors and ask what they pay for space.
But he still likes the opportunity.
"A small investor can still buy, but the deal has to work on rents you can collect today, not on what an institution might pay you later," Blankenship said.

articles.title: Heating oil prices are up 59% from last winter. The spike is 'crushing folks,' Maine nonprofit says
articles.text:
Winter heating bills can strain household budgets. This year, a spike in heating oil prices could make the season especially difficult for households that depend on the fuel and have little financial wiggle room.
The national average price of heating oil was roughly $5.91 a gallon as of Nov. 9, up about $2.19, or 59%, from a year earlier, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
In Maine, the average price per gallon is roughly $5.83, up about $2.49 from a year earlier, or about 75%. The state is among those whose residents may feel the price rise acutely — about 50% of homes there use heating oil.
The jump "is crushing folks," said Jason Parent, CEO of AVEC Community Action, a nonprofit agency based in Presque Isle, Maine, that provides heating assistance and other social services in three of the state's 16 counties. Many residents face immediate crises, he said, such as empty fuel tanks or reliance on unsafe heating sources.
"My fear is that there are households out there who have secondary fuel sources like wood stoves, pellet stoves and other things that are no longer operating and functioning in a safe way," Parent said.
The price surge comes on the heels of years of high overall inflation that has already squeezed household budgets, he said.
"The cost of living has made it impossible for households who had been figuring out how to get by without [financial help]," Parent said.
Why the price has jumped
The price spike comes amid a tight global market for refined fuels, a category that includes heating oil and diesel. Supply shocks tied to the Iran war and the Russia-Ukraine war, low inventories and limited refining capacity have constrained supplies and added upward pressure on fuel prices, according to recent research from the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City.
The EIA predicts that a warmer winter in the Northeast will reduce consumption, helping to offset higher prices. In October, the agency forecast that the average household using heating oil will spend $2,115 from November through March, about 21% more than last year.
Meanwhile, homes primarily heated with natural gas are expected to spend an average of $640 this winter, down 9%, while those using propane are forecast to spend an average of $1,246, down 3%, according to the EIA's October forecast. Households using electricity for heating are expected to spend an average of $1,196, up 4% from a year ago. These are national figures.
How residents seek financial help
Roughly 4.1 million U.S. households use heating oil as their primary means of heating their homes, according to the EIA. Most of them — close to 3.4 million — are located in the Northeast.
Unlike electricity or natural gas, heating oil is delivered in large quantities. Payment terms vary, but some dealers require a minimum delivery or charge extra for smaller orders. In Maine, for example, ordering at least 100 gallons for a standard 275-gallon tank can avoid a surcharge, according to the state attorney general's office. At current prices, that 100 gallons would cost about $600 — a tall order for some households.
AVEC's Home Energy Assistance Program, or HEAP, provides financial assistance to qualifying households, based primarily on income and the number of people living in the home. Funding originates with the federal Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, or LIHEAP, which is run by the U.S. Health and Human Services Department and overseen by state agencies, often working with local organizations such as AVEC.
Maine and tribal grantees in the state received about $38 million from LIHEAP in October, according to a press release from outgoing Republican Sen. Susan Collins. AVEC administers about $4 million of that through HEAP, Parent said. AVEC also gets donations from community fundraising to help residents cover heating costs.
A component of HEAP is the Energy Crisis Intervention Program, which serves qualifying families who face an energy crisis, such as a potential electric shutoff or an empty oil tank and no financial means to replenish the supply.
AVEC began taking calls for that program on Nov. 2, Parent said.
"In the first hour alone, there were 150 voicemail messages on our emergency fuel line," Parent said. "People were in crisis before the program opened up."
Charitable donations help residents in crisis
Catherine Lafleche of Hersey, Maine, describes AVEC as a lifeline.
The 65-year-old is guardian to two grandchildren, ages 11 and 6, and is living mostly on about $1,100 in monthly Social Security benefits and state guardianship assistance, after shattering her upper-arm bone in a fall in April. Her injury required reverse shoulder replacement surgery, from which she continues to recover. Before that fall, she had worked as a substitute teacher and bookkeeper.
"I'm $6,000 short of income at this point in the year," Lafleche said.
Hersey is in Maine's northernmost county, Aroostook, where January and February bring average high temperatures in the 20s and average lows in the single digits, based on National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration data from 1991 to 2020 recorded at a Caribou Municipal Airport weather station. Last winter, the area experienced severe cold snaps, including on Jan. 24, when the high was minus 2 degrees Fahrenheit.
When the oil man came, I cried.Catherine LaflecheResident of Hersey, Maine
Lafleche applied to HEAP through AVEC in August, but a backlog meant potentially waiting until November for assistance. Unable to afford more fuel when it became chilly, she ran out of heating oil in early October and relied on a small wood stove to keep part of her house warm, burning Amazon boxes collected from other local residents because she didn't have enough firewood.
In late October, an AVEC representative called to say a charitable donation would cover 100 gallons of heating oil.
"When the oil man came, I cried," Lafleche said.
Benefits through AVEC don't stretch as far this year
For residents in Maine who need help covering the cost to heat their homes and are seeking out help, "the need is outpacing the benefits," said Parent, of AVEC.
The average benefit through HEAP is about $750 per household this season, up from roughly $550 a year ago, Parent said. "That $750 is going less far than the $550 did last season" for heating oil, he said. "It's buying fewer gallons because of the precipitous increase."
The benefits are generally paid directly to the fuel supplier as a credit on the household's account. Even if a household qualifies, funding may run out.
"We're in a world of hurt now ... but it's going to be crisis time again in January or February," Parent said.
Trump administration takes step to bring down cost
The Trump administration, in an effort to bring down heating oil prices, said it would release 300,000 barrels of heating oil from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve, according to a Nov. 4 release from the U.S. Energy Department.
Whether adding this extra heating oil to the market will reduce prices for residents depends at least partly on how it gets doled out, said Jonathan Rubin, director of the Margaret Chase Smith Policy Center and a professor of economics at the University of Maine.
"No one really knows the economic impact, because will the home-heating oil distributors release it in one month, which would make it about 10% to 12% of a single month's supply? Or will they release it over the entire season, in which case it's only about one and a half percent of the entire season's home heating oil supply?" Rubin said.
"I would say that this is a modest short-term buffer," he said.
Lawmakers call for extra funding for heating assistance
Congressional lawmakers have called for increased LIHEAP funding this year due to rising energy costs, including heating oil. Dozens of House lawmakers — mostly Democrats — signed an Oct. 14 letter to the House Appropriations Committee seeking an additional $3 billion in emergency supplemental funding for LIHEAP.
That followed an Oct. 1 letter from a group of Democratic senators and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., to Robert F. Kennedy Jr., secretary of the Health and Human Services, also asking that he seek at least $3 billion more for LIHEAP.
Already, the government released roughly $3.63 billion in LIHEAP funding nationwide on Oct. 9 — 90% of the roughly $4 billion available under a continuing resolution that is currently funding federal agencies.
The timing for disbursing the remainder depends on when Congress either passes full-year funding for the 2027 fiscal year — which started Oct. 1 and runs through Sept. 30, 2027 — or passes another stopgap measure to keep the government running. If lawmakers do neither by Dec. 11, a federal shutdown would begin.
Whether the additional $3 billion requested for LIHEAP will be considered in any upcoming congressional appropriations process is uncertain.
Lafleche, the Hersey resident, said the 100 gallons of heating oil donated to her, along with some firewood she has now purchased, should keep her home warm until early December. She hopes to receive approval for benefits by then through HEAP, which has helped her in past years.
"We're not in this position by choice. Most of us made every plan to the contrary, but it stacked up to be not enough. And I feel like we don't deserve to be cold," she said.

Other companies rated buy at Bank of America and screened by CNBC Pro include: US Bancorp, Krispy Kreme , Madison Square Garden Entertainment and L3 Harris Technologies.
