articles.title: How Canadian stocks could be big winners of U.S. midterms
articles.text: Stock market winners out of the 2026 midterm elections could be emerging north of the U.S. border. The S & P/TSX Composite index , Canada's stock market benchmark, rose 2.3% the day after the U.S. elections, its best one-day performance since March 31. The index is also up 1.6% since the vote, while the S & P 500 has sagged 0.5% in that time. Democrats flipped eight Senate seats and more than 40 House seats to gain control of the U.S. Congress. Their newfound power on Capitol Hill is stoking confidence that the U.S. could adopt a softer stance on trade relations with Canada. Under the second Trump administration, the U.S. has banned several Canadian imports , while Canada has responded with tariffs and curbs of its own. Now, "there's optimism that something's going to change," said William Alan Reinsch, Scholl Chair in International Business at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a bipartisan policy research group. "That's based on the election returns, but also on statements by a number of Democrats ... that they intend to deal with Canadian tariffs." .GSPTSE mountain 2026-11-03 S & P TSX vs SP500 since midterms Canada has long counted the U.S. as its largest trading partner. In 2024, Canada sent 76% of its total export goods worth $596.1 billion to the U.S., according to Canadian government data . The country's top exports to the U.S. include raw aluminum, car parts, crude petroleum, and paper and wood pulp, per international trade data platform The Observatory of Economic Complexity. That historically warm relationship has chilled over the past two years — and it's had critical consequences for Canada and its markets. The iShares MSCI Canada ETF (EWC) plunged 5.4% on April 4, 2025, two days after President Donald Trump unveiled sweeping tariffs against a slew of countries, including Canada, in what he called "liberation day." And in July, Trump announced additional 50% levies on certain Canadian imports such as dairy products, alcoholic beverages and motor vehicle parts, sparking sell-offs in some stocks. "Investors have fears about global trade and global complexities, and that likely [has] led to some selling off of those stocks," Chris White, head of research at Canada-based investment firm 5i Research, told CNBC. He noted that swaths of Canadian stocks have been battered by U.S. tariffs, even though the Toronto Stock Exchange outperformed in 2025 because it is largely composed of energy companies and gold miners that have benefited from mounting geopolitical uncertainty tied to Trump's tenure. Democrats take on Trump's tariffs There are signs that a more heavily Democratic Congress will tackle Trump's tariffs next year , creating new opportunities for investors in Canadian stocks, according to Justus Parmar, founder and CEO of Fortuna Investments. "There's going to be a real big pushback from the Democrats [on tariffs]," Parmar told CNBC. "We're seeing some really big kinds of opportunities in Canada to start deploying money." Democrats have already proposed a few measures to rewrite federal trade laws, which could reverse the U.S.' tariffs against Canada and limit Trump and future presidents' abilities to unilaterally impose new ones. In September, Sens. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., and Peter Welch, D-Vt., put forth the Banning Antiquated Duties and Delivering Equitable American Levies Act, or BAD DEAL Act, to "repeal all tariffs levied under Section 338 of the Tariff Act " and refund Americans for duties paid under the authority, including those brought against Canada. There is still some room for the president to negotiate those tariffs down, try and get a [reputational] win with his remaining voters. finance professor at the University at Buffalo School of Management Scott Laing U.S. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan is one of several incoming lawmakers who have also criticized Trump's tariffs and vowed to tackle them. However, Scott Laing, finance professor at the University at Buffalo School of Management, noted Democrats won't have enough representation in Congress to completely neutralize the president's powers on trade. "The Democrats have the majority, but they don't have a supermajority," Laing added. "So, the tariffs are ultimately in the hands of the president." Even so, Trump looks more likely than ever to change his tune on tariffs, following Republicans' losses in the midterm elections, which were largely viewed as a referendum on his administration's policies. "There is still some room for the president to negotiate those tariffs down, try and get a [reputational] win with his remaining voters," Laing said. "He's aware that they need to come down and get costs lower for consumers, so I wouldn't be surprised if they did come down a bit ... tariffs are an easy way to kind of give him an ability to lower [costs] and preserve his legacy." How to play it There are several ways investors can position themselves in Canadian stocks to ride the tailwinds of an expected U.S. trade policy shift. White, of 5i Research, noted that Magna International and Linamar Corporation — two major automotive parts manufacturers — could see some upside from tariff relief. Both companies are reliant on business with the U.S. because the Canadian and American car industries are heavily integrated, Laing said. Other companies that rely heavily on stateside sales, such as Canada Goose and Molson Coors , are also likely to surge following any such relief, Laing said. Molson Coors has plunged more than 30% since Trump's tariffs were first publicized, while Canada Goose has traded roughly flat. Ontario-based Algoma Steel Group , a producer of hot- and cold-rolled steel sheet and plate products, should also see considerable upside from improved U.S.-Canada trade relations, White said. "With the tariffs, their share of U.S. sales declined" from more than 50% to less than 25%, limiting Algoma's share growth, White noted. Late last year, the company also cut 1,000 workers , citing pressures from U.S. tariffs. Shares of the steelmaker have traded roughly flat since Trump's "liberation day." White also noted that several Canada-based software stocks, including Descartes Systems Group , could get a boost as the Democratic gains give way to more predictable geopolitical conditions that should encourage investors to spread their dollars more widely. "In times of fear and great uncertainty, Canadian investors sometimes flee to those larger [Canada-based] banks just because they've been so resilient over the years," White told CNBC. "That kind of took capital out of the software trade." Shares of Descartes are down nearly 9% since April 2, 2025, offering a good entry point to investors, the researcher said.

articles.title: Juice your growth and save on taxes in this workplace investment account
articles.text:
Workers are in the heart of open enrollment season for next year's benefits, and rising healthcare costs are shining a spotlight on an offering that includes a tax-advantaged investment account.
Healthcare expenses are climbing for workers and employers alike, with average total family premiums, including the employer's share, averaging $28,303, up 5% from a year ago, according to data from health policy organization KFF, formerly the Kaiser Family Foundation.
To manage the costs, a growing number of employers are moving to high-deductible health plans, which work alongside health savings accounts or HSAs. Almost 40% of companies with at least 10 employees that offer health benefits also have an HSA-qualified plan, KFF found.
Health savings accounts have three major tax advantages. First, contributions that your employer automatically deducts from your pay aren't taxed. Second, money stashed into the HSA grows free of taxes. Finally, you can make tax-free withdrawals for qualified health expenses – just be sure to save your receipts.
"I love HSAs because of their triple-tax advantage," said Eileen Olson, CFP and founder of Emerald Wealth in Daufuskie Island, South Carolina, near Savannah, Georgia. "For people who can afford to leave it alone, it can be one of the best retirement accounts they're going to have."
Money for the long run
In 2027, those with individual healthcare coverage through a high-deductible plan can stash up to $4,500 in an HSA, including any contributions from employers. That number goes up to $9,000 for family plans. Individuals can kick in a catch-up contribution of $1,000 if they're aged 55 and older and not enrolled in Medicare.
The HSA differs from the healthcare flexible spending account, known as the FSA.
FSA funds must be used by the end of the plan year unless your employer allows a carryover of up to $700 or an additional 2.5 months to use the money. HSAs, however, have no expiration date on their funds – and that's what makes them such a powerful tool for long-term planning. You can also take the HSA with you if you change employers.
"Get the money deployed, take advantage of the pretax contribution, and allocate the money into a growth portfolio," said Mark Stancato, certified financial planner at VIP Wealth Advisors in Decatur, Georgia. "With the HSA, you can keep compounding year over year."
Optimizing your account
The structure of an HSA and the available investment menu will vary from one plan to the next, and some will require that employees keep some of their holdings in cash.
Preset HSA fund menus tend to have 15 to 25 funds to choose from, and providers say that accountholders who invest tend to use two to four funds, according to Greg Carlson, senior research analyst for equity strategies at Morningstar.
How you allocate your HSA will depend on several factors, including your family's health prospects in the next year, your cash flow needs – how much you can comfortably sock into the HSA – and your risk tolerance, said André Small, CFP and founder of A Small Investment in Houston.
Health savings accounts contributions and plan info for 2027
| Category | Self-only coverage | Family coverage | 
|---|---|---|
| Annual contribution limit | $4,500 | $9,000 | 
| Catch-up contribution (age 55+) | $1,000 | $1,000 | 
| Annual high-deductible plan deductible limit | No less than $1,750 | No less than $3,500 | 
| Annual out-of-pocket expenses | No more than $8,700 | No more than $17,400 | 
Source: Internal Revenue Service
Small's standard is to keep an amount equal to 120% of the plan's out-of-pocket maximum held in cash in the HSA.
"That covers a bad year without forcing a sale at the wrong time," he said. "Above that amount? I typically advise investing the amount the client is comfortable investing, allocated to their risk tolerance, their time horizon and the goal of spending these dollars on care later."
For 2027, the IRS defines a high-deductible plan as one with an annual deductible no less than $1,750 for self-only coverage ($3,500 for family plans) and with an out-of-pocket expense limit that doesn't exceed $8,700 for self-only (or $17,400 for family coverage). Out-of-pocket expenses include deductibles, copays and other costs – but not premiums.
Growth oriented
Other advisors suggest having up to the deductible in cash, though some HSA plan providers require a stated minimum amount in cash.
Beyond this cash reserve, financial advisors recommend allocating into stocks.
Patrick Swift, CFP and president of Amplius Wealth Advisors in Blue Bell, Pennsylvania, aims for an allocation of up to 60% in U.S. large cap stocks, 20% in small and mid-cap stocks and 20% in international stocks.
"We believe the equity portfolio should be well diversified," he said. "If the [HSA] balance is 2% to 10% of your net worth, why not be aggressive? That can change based on the situation, but if you are comfortable with the philosophical aspect, why not be growth oriented?"
Similarly, Stancato likes to go heavy on equity exposure in HSA accounts. "I allocate more dollars into small caps and emerging markets – those asset classes with more volatility but also more opportunity for growth," the advisor said. He also adds some large-cap domestic exposure.
For the adventurous, select HSA providers are offering brokerage window access, meaning investors can pick from a broader array of investments, including individual stocks.
This year, seven providers surveyed by Morningstar offer access to brokerage windows – up from four in 2023 – including HealthEquity, Fidelity and Lively. Be aware that there may be annual fees attached, either a flat dollar amount or a percentage of assets.
Rachel Elson, a CFP and wealth advisor at Perigon Wealth Management in San Francisco, recommends keeping things simple. "You can do a three-ETF model, covering some allocation that includes the U.S. market, and two ETFs for developed and emerging markets."
"You don't need to get super complicated here," she added.

articles.title: Berkshire breaks out to record high with fourth-quarter rally reaching 19%
articles.text:
(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)
Even more record highs as Berkshire's Q4 rally scores 19% gain
Berkshire Hathaway's red-hot shares are ending a strong week with four consecutive fresh record high closes.
Since the rally began with the start of the fourth quarter on October 1, the Class A shares have closed at record highs 11 times as they soared 19.1%.
The much more widely held B shares closed at new highs just 10 times but are also up 19.1% from their near-term low.
The gains are in sharp contrast to the S&P 500's 1.2% dip as investors appear to be seeing Berkshire as a relatively safe haven amid worries about AI stocks and spending.
Both Berkshire classes were up 3.9% on the week as the S&P advanced by 2.5%, its best week since early August.
Berkshire's B shares are now 7.5 percentage points ahead of the benchmark for the year so far.
After erasing their post-Buffett CEO announcement losses three weeks ago, Berkshire shares are now up almost 10% since last year's shareholders meeting.
They've gained around 29% since last August's lows and are up around 18% year-to-date.
Financials filing points to more Bank of America sales
Berkshire Hathaway is due to disclose its quarterly equity portfolio snapshot on Monday when it files its Q3 13F with the SEC.
We won't know for sure until then, but numbers in the company's third quarter 10-Q, released last Saturday, indicate Berkshire continued to reduce its Bank of America stake.
It would be the ninth consecutive quarter of selling.
As of June 30, Berkshire reported holding 483.4 million BAC shares valued now at $24.7 billion, it's fifth largest equity position.
On June 30, 2024, before the selling began, Berkshire owned just over 1 billion shares valued at $41.1 billion.
Since then, the number of shares in the portfolio has decreased by 53.2%, not including any Q3 sales, while the stock price has increased by 28.3%.
If there had been no reductions, the position would be worth $52.7 billion.
The belief Berkshire sold more BAC shares in the third quarter is based on a $372 million reduction in the cost basis for equities categorized by the company as "banks, insurance, and finance."
The 10-Q also reports $2.2 billion of pretax gains from equity sales.
Barron's notes Bank of America and American Express are the only financial stocks in the portfolio that have a cost basis low enough to generate a gain like that. Amex is one of the four stocks new CEO Greg Abel indicated would be held for "decades" to come in his February letter to shareholders.
In any case, Berkshire's almost 23% stake in Amex would have required it to quickly disclose any sales.
Based on the numbers in the 10-Q, the warrants Berkshire received as part of a 2011 $5 billion investment in the bank that it used in 2017 to buy 700 million shares at $7.14 each, and BAC's average stock price in the quarter, Barron's estimates 30 to 40 million shares may have been sold.
That would be roughly in line with the 30.2 million shares sold in the second quarter.
The case isn't as good, but Barron's thinks Berkshire may have bought more Alphabet shares in the period. That's based on a $2.3 billion increase in the cost basis for the category that includes Google's parent.
Overall, it looks like it will be a relatively quiet quarter with $2.4 billion in equity purchases and $2.8 billion in sales.
In the first quarter, Berkshire bought $15.9 billion and sold $24.1 billion of equities. In the second quarter, it purchased $23.5 billion and sold $3.7 billion.
All those numbers exclude the company's buybacks of its own stock.
Second yen bond sale of the year offers more attractive rates
In a term sheet filed early Friday, Berkshire Hathaway says it is selling more than 182 billion yen ($1.1 billion) worth of bonds with maturities between 2029 and 2056 and annual interest rates between 2.6% and 4.6%.
Bloomberg points out the rates, compared to benchmarks, are higher than its previous sale this year.
It quotes a fund manager as saying market sentiment "has become more sensitive," forcing issuers to make their offerings more attractive.
In April, Berkshire sold 272 billion yen ($1.7 billion) of bonds.
Berkshire uses the proceeds from the yen-denominated bonds to protect its ongoing investments in Japanese stocks from currency fluctuations.
BUFFETT & BERKSHIRE AROUND THE INTERNET
Some links may require a subscription:
- Barron's on MSN: Berkshire's Geico unit struggles despite turnaround; its profitability trails Progressive
- Business Insider on MSN: Warren Buffett isn't running Berkshire anymore. You wouldn't know it.
HIGHLIGHTS FROM CNBC'S BUFFETT ARCHIVE
Buffett lists Ben Graham's three vital investing principles (1996)
Warren Buffett recommends Benjamin Graham's book, "The Intelligent Investor," and outlines what he considers Graham's three most important ideas.
WARREN BUFFETT: On investment books, if you're asking about that, I would recommend the first two books that Phil Fisher wrote back around 1960, "Common Sense [Stocks] and Uncommon Profits" and the second one ["Paths to Wealth Through Common Stocks"]. They're very good books.
You know, I obviously recommend, first and foremost, [Benjamin Graham's] "The Intelligent Investor," with chapters eight and 20 are the ones that you really should read.
Two of the — well, all of the important ideas in investing, really, are in that book, because there's only about three ideas. And those — two of them are emphasized in those two chapters...
One is that — to think of yourself — to think of investing as owning a business and not buying something that wiggles around in price.
And the second one is your attitude, which ties in with that, the attitude toward the market, that's covered in chapter eight. And if you have the proper attitude toward market movements, it's an enormous help in securities.
And the final chapter is on the margin of safety, which means, don't try and drive a 9,800-pound truck over a bridge that says it's, you know, "Capacity: 10,000 pounds." But go down the road a little bit and find one that says, "Capacity: 15,000 pounds."

articles.title: How Rockstar's 'GTA VI' release could reshape gaming, streaming and even paid time off
articles.text:
It's been 13 years since the last installment of Grand Theft Auto, and fans are getting ready for what analysts say could be the biggest video game launch of all time.
The latest game in the franchise, "Grand Theft Auto VI," is set to launch on Nov. 19, after Take-Two Interactive's Rockstar Games delayed its launch twice. Roth analyst Eric Handler estimated the game maker spent more than $1 billion developing the game.
Sales figures could end up breaking records. Sensor Tower estimated over 12 million preorders through Nov. 13, and Morgan Stanley forecast the game could sell 40 million copies by March 2027.
Beyond launch week, the Grand Theft Auto, or GTA, franchise has a track record of lasting engagement over many years. Even 13 years after launch, "Grand Theft Auto V" is one of the top five most viewed games on Twitch this year.
In anticipation of the game's launch, investors have been taking note: Take-two's stock has more than doubled since the beginning of 2023.
The release is seen as not only a monumental moment for developer Rockstar Games and parent company Take-Two, but also a massive opportunity for the entire gaming industry.
Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick addressed demand in a recent "Squawk Box" interview, saying, "We tend to be pretty judicious when we talk about this sort of thing, but our expectations were high and they are being vastly exceeded so far."
Streamers and creators across the digital ecosystem are looking at the launch as a massive opportunity to drive engagement with their content and fuel subscriber and ad revenue growth.
A creator who goes by the name Deansocool, who has 375,000 followers on Twitch and posts content to YouTube and other social platforms as well, said "GTA VI" will enable creators to grow their audience and provide a massive opportunity for newer streamers to make a name for themselves.
"This game is going to make a lot of millionaires in 2027. A lot of creators gotta understand this is it. This is that golden ticket. This is like a hundred times bigger than Fortnite," he said in an interview with CNBC.
"It goes beyond this launch moment into this sustaining opportunity for them to grow, build, engage and retain their audience and ultimately support themselves by making money," said Twitch Chief Product Officer Mike Minton.
GTA PTO
The release of the latest Grand Theft Auto title could draw so much attention that its impact will be felt beyond just the world of gaming.
BambooHR, a workplace time-off platform, reported that paid time off requests for the "GTA VI" release date are nearly 13% higher than equivalent days in 2024 and 2025. It also noted that nearly one in five workers are planning to take time off for the launch.
PwC issued a report examining all the different sectors of the economy that could benefit from the game's launch — or be hurt by it. The firm projected that food delivery companies could see a surge from hunkered-down gamers, and Miami tourism could benefit. PwC noted that foreign visitors to Seoul's Bukchon Hanok Village, which inspired a location in the hit Netflix movie KPop Demon Hunters, increased 118% in the four weeks following the movie's debut.
Music streaming also looks set to get a boost. Tom Petty's "Love Is a Long Road," which appeared in the first "GTA VI" trailer in December 2023, reportedly saw Spotify streams jump by more than 37,000%.
On the downside, the game could distract from movies and streaming entertainment.
"How are people spending Thanksgiving? There's a lot of sports on TV, but you've also got a pretty solid group of your demographics that are going to be focused on playing 'GTA VI,'" said Bart Spiegel, who leads PwC's Global Entertainment & Media sector. "You're going to start to pull eyeballs away from video streaming platforms.
"I think you're going to hear a lot of analyst calls in the first quarter of 2027 saying, 'Hey, listen, some of our numbers were down because of the release of this game,'" Spiegel added.
Rockstar Games declined CNBC's interview request. Watch the video above to learn more.

articles.title: Family offices see more upside in smaller startup bets
articles.text:
A version of this article appeared in CNBC's Inside Wealth newsletter, a weekly guide to the high-net-worth investor and consumer. Sign up to receive future editions straight to your inbox.
Investors are racing to meet artificial-intelligence companies' massive capital needs, writing larger checks to fewer startups. Megadeals, or rounds of at least $100 million, made up a whopping 87.5% of U.S. venture capital deployed in the first half of 2026, according to PitchBook.
But some family offices are bucking the trend, seeking outsized returns from smaller bets on younger companies.
"I think there's a big misconception that writing large checks into these late-stage rounds de-risks investments," said Jason Blanck, an investor who started his namesake family office in 2024. "In reality, they're paying essentially peak market multiples and slower growth, so they're not really getting much upside."
For family offices that invest for generations, waiting longer for a larger relative return on investment is worth it, according to John Morrissey, managing director of Shea Ventures. The Shea family, whose construction company helped build the Golden Gate Bridge and the Hoover Dam, has invested in venture capital since the late 1960s.
"Our goal is to sustain our wealth and to grow it tax efficiently and generationally," Morrissey said. "If I have one investment that can continue to compound in the double digits, that's almost inevitably better than something invested for a short period with a very high return and sends me back the money. Then I have to go try to find something else."
He looks for funds with limited partners who, like Shea Ventures, prioritize the investment multiple over the internal rate of return. Large institutional investors and sovereign wealth funds, on the other hand, often want capital returned sooner and have different tax considerations, according to Morrissey. He added that they can typically afford to make bigger allocations to one round or asset class than most family offices.
"Family offices like those of David Rubenstein or Josh Harris, those are the exception. Most family offices may have a couple of billion dollars, and maybe you have an operating business that you've got to feed," Morrissey said. "You're never going to be able to participate at the same level as Yale's endowment."
He also views early-stage funds as more closely aligned with the family office's investment goals. Managers investing in late-stage mega rounds can earn substantial carry by securing access and riding a company's momentum. Funds that invest in smaller firms, he said, need their investments to grow at much higher multiples to earn that incentive income.
Shea Ventures backs startups through direct investments and funds such as Shakti. The five-year-old fund backs startups at inception, sometimes before they even have a product or revenue.
"There are healthy, meaning low, valuations available if one is willing to be unconventional and not afraid to not be part of the herd," said Shakti partner and founder Keval Desai.
Shakti backs AI-related startups but finds attractive entry points by looking for less crowded niches, Desai said. For instance, the fund's portfolio includes two robotics companies that collect garbage, with one focused on space.
Shea Ventures and Blanck Capital both balance their risk by also investing in growth equity. Blanck describes it as a barbell approach, with venture assets like direct early-stage investments and secondaries making up a minority of the portfolio, alongside a core base of public equities.
He has invested in Anthropic but is more excited to talk about less buzzy startups in his portfolio like Longshot Space Technology, which is building what the company calls a "space gun" to shoot payloads into orbit. Blanck Capital has backed Longshot since its pre-seed round in 2023, and it has since secured contracts with the U.S. Air Force, DARPA and the U.S. Navy.
"I'm invested in Anthropic, but it doesn't mean it's going to be the best investment of my year or portfolio," Blanck said. "It might be the most popular, or might get the most attention with other investors or friends and industry folks, but it's not moving the needle for me, let me just put it that way."

articles.title: Retailers are turning to entertainment to win shoppers’ attention
articles.text:
Legacy retailer Gap Inc. made an unconventional hire earlier this year: a chief entertainment officer.
It was a newly created role as the company tapped former Paramount executive Pam Kaufman to helm its entertainment, content and licensing platform. Gap has since rolled out major campaigns, partnering with bands like Just Your Type and building on the success of last year's ads with girl group Katseye.
"Beloved brands have value beyond the products they sell. Consumers identify with them, trust them and want to be part of their world," Kaufman told CNBC in a statement. "The key is authenticity: Every extension has to reflect what the brand stands for and give its fans a meaningful new way to experience it."
She said it's part of a broader goal to emphasize what Gap calls "fashiontainment," a strategy to blend retail and entertainment to better align with consumers. Gap is part of a growing cohort of retailers investing in entertainment and experiences both in-store and through exclusive online content to drive engagement.
"Brands are stories, and we are the storytellers," CEO Richard Dickson said at the Goldman Sachs Global Consumer and Retail conference in September. "I think you could see that come to life when you look at some of the work that we've done, putting our brands in the center of culture and cultural conversation."
In another blending of retail and media, Mattel made waves a few years ago for its "Barbie" movie, building on the intellectual property of a decades-old fan favorite and drawing in massive box office success. At the time, Dickson was president and chief operating officer of the company, witnessing firsthand the sectors' intersection before departing for Gap.
"I think the post-Covid consumer attitude around shopping certainly evolved a lot," said Bryan Eshelman, who leads the retail practice at consulting firm AlixPartners. "It has gone from shopping as a fulfillment task to shopping, in many instances, more as an entertainment form."
Between experiences in physical stores and media campaigns featuring exclusive content, Eshelman said, retailers are getting more creative about the ways they're driving engagement and marketing.
"Community, at the end of the day, is one of the key ways to drive loyalty, so I think retailers of all types are trying to tap into some sense of community, some sense of lifestyle, some sense of belonging that's beyond the product that they offer," he said.
Branded entertainment has been around for a long time. Procter & Gamble made headlines in the 1930s for helping to coin the term "soap opera," and companies have for decades created media campaigns to draw in customers.
But with the rise of social media, content creation and short-form offerings, experts said audiences are becoming hungrier than ever for something new and original.
Valuable IP wins
The retail and entertainment intersection is happening at a time when intellectual property is becoming more valuable than ever, according to experts.
As consumers encounter more marketing than ever, the companies that will win the battle for attention are the ones that can "cut through all of the noise," said Alex Michael, senior managing director at investment firm LionTree.
"The hardest thing to find and to get is audience these days," Michael told CNBC. "IP, in that sense, is the most valuable thing out there, and only becoming more valuable because it's attached to audience."
At the same time, he said, the way IP is distributed is broadening to include video, audio, short-form, long-form and live event content. Consumers are also redefining their loyalty to brands, which means companies have to "play much earlier in the consumer journey" than they have in years past to secure their trust, he said.
The trend is also likely helped by executives who have worked in both retail and entertainment: Gap's Kaufman came from Paramount, for example, and Dickson and Skydance co-CEO Ynon Kreiz held top roles at Mattel.
"The gray areas have never been more pronounced as to what is classically defined as retail or media or entertainment or live events," Michael said. "People who have cross-sector expertise are increasingly more valuable because you can't be defined by a single vertical, especially as things change so quickly."
Bridging the gap
Still, there's room for newer players, especially with the studio landscape rapidly changing, said Sean Akaks, the CEO of SonderCo, an agency that partners brands with celebrities and entertainment properties.
"I think it's a really interesting time for nontraditional players to be making content because you're seeing this massive consolidation of these legacy entertainment companies," he said. "I think there are just more open lanes for independent creators and also brands and anyone outside the traditional studio system to create content."
That's where retailers might tap creators, Akaks said, because they can use their platforms to reach consumers directly.
"I do think there's a world where we're going to see creators and brands sort of co-creating IP that maybe they're owning together," he said.
Once those companies get consumers into the store, they're also leaning into experiential retail, making shopping a more immersive experience than it otherwise would be, like Dick's Sporting Goods offering interactive activities and simulators in its stores.
According to data from AlixPartners, companies investing in experiential retail such as Coach and Ralph Lauren saw close to 10% year-over-year increases in consumers' average basket size.
"The idea that retailers would potentially invest in some distributed electronic content to help drive traffic, and then when you get there, it's experiential — it really goes into the kinds of flywheels that entertainment companies are also trying to build and grow," said Jeff Goldstein, co-lead of the media and entertainment practice at AlixPartners.
Yet, the entertainment that retail brands are developing is only one piece in a larger puzzle to retain customers and attract new ones. Translating that into tangible sales growth isn't necessarily a given.
"The basics of having great product in stock at a transparent price that feels like value is not swept away by animatronics," AlixPartners' Eshelman said. "The fundamentals are still there, and if you're going to have a good retail proposition, you need to have that balance. You can't mask bad product at a bad price with no inventory with glitz and glamour."

articles.title: Meet the seven co-founders of Anthropic
articles.text:
Four researchers, a former journalist, a public policymaker, and an engineer founded Anthropic in 2021. Six years later, the artificial intelligence company is about to go public, with trading expected to begin on Nov. 19, in what will be one of the biggest IPOs on record.
Those seven co-founders are poised to each be worth many billions of dollars.
It all started with a defection.
At the end of 2020, siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei were vice presidents at OpenAI, the company that kicked off the generative AI frenzy with the launch of ChatGPT. But the two had grown frustrated with their employer over its approach to AI safety. Fearing a world where AI models' capabilities would progress faster than our understanding of them, the duo launched Anthropic early the next year.
They took a handful of OpenAI colleagues with them: Tom Brown, the company's research engineering lead on GPT-3; Jack Clark, a policy director; Jared Kaplan, a contract research consultant; and Sam McCandlish and Chris Olah, both members of OpenAI's technical staff.
They were all deeply concerned about OpenAI's ambitions to focus on commercialization, and they now stand to be some of the first to cash in on the AI boom.
"They really started Anthropic not because they were hoping to get rich, but they started Anthropic because they like wanted to shape this really important thing in the world, and they thought that other people might do it worse than them," said Jeffrey Ladish, who joined Anthropic as a contract safety engineer in September 2021, and now serves as the executive director of AI safety institute Palisade Research.
Collectively the co-founders own about 10% of Anthropic. Each has about 240,000,000 class A shares, or about a 1.4% stake.
During Anthropic's most recent funding round, those shares — valued at $58.90 each — amounted to about $14 billion in value for each co-founder. If Anthropic's IPO reaches its target of $70 to $78 per share, or a market valuation of nearly $1.4 trillion, it would push those stakes to $17 billion to $18 billion.
"It's extremely hard not to be influenced by your incentives," Ladish said. "You have investors, and money is not just like an end; it's also a means."
Anthropic did not respond to requests for comment.
Dario Amodei
The face of Anthropic is CEO Dario Amodei. He holds the most shares of the bunch: 245,259,100 including shares subject to voting proxies.
Amodei, 43, didn't get his start in business. He comes from the world of research, obtaining a doctorate in computational neuroscience from Princeton University in 2011. He then went to work at Stanford University as a postdoctoral scholar from 2011 to 2014.
Even in the private sector, Amodei's experience was focused on research. He worked at China's Baidu, leading research on speech recognition from 2014 to 2015, followed by a stint at Google Brain working on deep learning and neural networks, foundational scientific frameworks for today's large language models. He joined OpenAI in July 2016.
On the Big Technology podcast in July 2025, Amodei said he got into AI to solve the "almost intractable" and "slow moving" problems of biology.
"I think my reason to start a company was that I had worked at other companies and I just didn't feel like the way those companies were run was really oriented towards trying to have that impact," he said, adding that the desire for impact was often used by companies as an insincere ploy to recruit talent.
At OpenAI, Amodei is credited with co-inventing reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), alongside Anthropic co-founder, Tom Brown. RLHF is a fine-tuning method used to align model outputs with human needs. That could mean training a model to speak politely or to not offer violent or harmful solutions to problems.
Daniela Amodei
Four years her brother's junior, Daniela Amodei, 39, serves as the president and board chair of Anthropic. The Amodeis are both San Francisco natives, growing up in the Mission District, just a few miles away from Anthropic's current headquarters.
The pair were teenagers during the height of the dot-com bubble and its subsequent fallout, both attending Lowell High School, a magnet school and one of the most prestigious public schools in the country. After graduating, Daniela went on to study English literature and politics at the University of California, Santa Cruz, earning her degree in 2009.
Daniela started her career in politics, working for Matt Cartwright, a Democrat representing what was then Pennsylvania's 17th congressional district, and then moved into tech, taking on various roles in risk management at Stripe for five years.
In a June interview with Stanford's Graduate School of Business, she said her experience in politics, specifically campaigns, naturally led her to startups and Silicon Valley.
"I was like, 'Wow, a small number of people that work really hard, who are young and driven, can really change the world,'" she said.
Tom Brown
Anthropic's chief compute officer, Tom Brown, 39, is perhaps the most entrepreneurial of the bunch. After graduating from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology with a Master of Engineering in 2010, Brown went on to found two startups, MoPub and Grouper.
MoPub was a mobile advertising business acquired by Twitter in 2013. There he served as founding engineer in 2011. Grouper, where Brown served as co-founder and technology chief, was a Y Combinator-backed group dating app.
After Grouper, Brown pivoted to research, sharing on Y Combinator's Lightcone podcast in August 2025 that he was self-taught on machine learning research, a daunting task since he received a B- in linear algebra at university.
"I kind of flip-flopped on it for six months trying to build up courage to" make the switch, he said.
Alongside co-inventing RLHF, as a researcher at OpenAI, Brown led the training efforts on GPT-3, a model that marked a historic leap from GPT-2, going from 1.5 billion parameters to 175 billion.
Jack Clark
Jack Clark, 37, the head of public benefit at Anthropic, left his career as a journalist in 2016 to work at OpenAI. Clark is now also the leader of the Anthropic Institute, the company's internal think tank that explores AI's social and economic impacts.
A native of the U.K., Clark grew up in the seaside town of Brighton and later studied English literature and creative writing at the University of East Anglia. He then went on to write for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg.
In an email to a colleague at Bloomberg at the time, Clark said his decision to leave journalism was because he had "never believed in something strongly before" and that he needed to join OpenAI "and live with the consequences, which I hope are good."
Jared Kaplan
Kaplan, 42, Anthropic's chief science officer, still holds a position as an associate professor in the department of physics and astronomy at Johns Hopkins University. The theoretical physicist got his PhD in physics from Harvard in 2009, working for four years after as a postdoctoral fellow at the SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, a particle physics research facility run by Stanford and funded by the Department of Energy.
Kaplan co-pioneered scaling laws, or the notion that large language models get exponentially better when trained on larger and larger data sets, alongside Dario Amodei. He also pioneered "constitutional AI," or a method of aligning models by using a list of safety principles and policies. His day-to-day work concerns safety assessments for models, responsible scaling policy at the company, and existential risks.
In an interview with The Guardian in December 2025, Kaplan noted that the decision over whether or not to let AI "recursively self improve," or write the code to enhance itself without a human in the loop, would be "in some ways the ultimate risk, because it's kind of like letting AI kind of go," and that he expects this risk will be taken sometime between 2027 and 2030.
Sam McCandlish
Anthropic's chief architect, Sam McCandlish, 36, came to OpenAI as a fellow focused on AI safety. He also led early research on coding tool Codex, which now constitutes a significant portion of OpenAI's revenue.
McCandlish claims he and the rest of the Anthropic co-founders were not following an entrepreneurial spirit when they charted out on their own. In a December 2024 video from Anthropic's YouTube channel, he said, "None of us wanted to found a company. We just felt like it was our duty."
McCandlish, like Kaplan, also came from the world of academia, completing his PhD in theoretical and mathematical physics at Stanford in 2017 and working at Boston University as a postdoctoral fellow the year afterward. His work focused on quantum gravity and tensor networks.
Now, his work focuses on pre-training, or the first step of training a large language model on swaths of data, among other things.
Chris Olah
Chris Olah, 34, heads Anthropic's interpretability research, a branch of study in machine learning that attempts to understand how a large language model "thinks" — or rather, which data inputs and reasoning methods it uses to arrive at its outputs.
Like McCandlish, Olah was not originally keen on starting a company. In the same December 2024 YouTube video, Olah said, "I was arguing for a long time that we should do a nonprofit instead, and just focus on safety research."
Olah had a nontraditional path to Anthropic, dropping out of the University of Toronto after one year and working for short stints as a developer at the government agency Environment Canada and software startup Xelerance.
His career truly took off when he was awarded a Thiel Fellowship in 2012, which he used to pursue research pertaining to 3D printers for two years. He then joined Google Brain, first as an intern and then as a researcher, before moving to OpenAI in 2018.
Majority voting control
While together the seven founders may only own about 10% of total equity, they will have a majority vote. Founder LLC, the legal entity set up that owns a single Class F share, gives Anthropic's co-founders a 50.1% majority voting control over the company. While Benjamin Mann, a member of Anthropic's technical staff and also an ex-OpenAI employee, is often called a co-founder, he is not an owner of Founder LLC.
The co-founders are expected to collectively sell over 20 million shares during the IPO, resulting in roughly $250 million in cash per founder, according to Anthropic's prospectus.
They plan to dedicate 80% of the wealth from their personal Anthropic equity to philanthropy, according to the IPO filing, though the pledge isn't legally binding. Anthropic is also setting aside 5% of its shares to form a new public benefit fund — to finance nonprofits, research, and potentially direct community grants — with potential to grow the size of the fund as the company itself grows.

articles.title: Con gái Chủ tịch Thép Nam Kim đăng ký mua 5 triệu cổ phiếu NKG
articles.text:
Con gái Chủ tịch Thép Nam Kim đăng ký mua 5 triệu cổ phiếu NKG
Bà Hồ Uyển Nhi, con gái ông Hồ Minh Quang - Chủ tịch HĐQT Thép Nam Kim đăng ký mua mua 5 triệu cổ phiếu NKG trong thời gian từ ngày 18/11 đến ngày 16/12/2026.
CTCP Thép Nam Kim (mã: NKG, sàn HoSE) vừa công bố đăng ký giao dịch cổ phiếu của người liên quan đến người nội bộ là bà Hồ Uyển Nhi, con gái ông Hồ Minh Quang - Chủ tịch HĐQT.
Cụ thể, bà Hồ Uyển Nhi đăng ký mua 5 triệu cổ phiếu NKG để nâng sở hữu từ 0%, lên 1,02% vốn điều lệ, thời gian giao dịch dự kiến từ ngày 18/11 đến ngày 16/12/2026.
Trước đó, con trai Chủ tịch Hồ Minh Quang là ông Hồ Minh Phát đã mua vào thành công 5 triệu cổ phiếu NKG trong khoảng thời gian từ ngày 17/4/2026 đến ngày 23/4/2026.
Sau giao dịch, ông Phát đã tăng sở hữu cổ phiếu NKG từ 5 triệu cổ phiếu lên 10 triệu cổ phiếu, tương tương tỷ lệ sở hữu tăng từ 1,12% lên 2,23% vốn tại Thép Nam Kim.
Được biết, Chủ tịch Hồ Minh Quang đang sở hữu hơn 78,1 triệu cổ phiếu NKG (tỷ lệ 15,87%).
Tương tự, Phó Tổng giám đốc Nguyễn Minh Khoa cũng đăng ký mua vào 100.000 cổ phiếu NKG trong thời gian từ 29/10 đến 26/11/2026 nhằm nâng sở hữu từ 0% lên 0,02%.
Về hoạt động kinh doanh, trong quý III/2026, Thép Nam Kim ghi nhận doanh thu thuần 5.472 tỷ đồng, tăng 45% so với cùng kỳ. Trừ đi giá vốn, lợi nhuận gộp tăng 175% so với cùng kỳ, lên 494,5 tỷ đồng
Trong kỳ, doanh thu tài chính tăng 27%, lên 66 tỷ đồng; chi phí tài chính tăng 89%, lên 121 tỷ đồng. Chi phí bán hàng và quản lý doanh nghiệp tăng 135%, lên tổng cộng 256 tỷ đồng. Qua đó, lợi nhuận sau thuế đạt 127,6 tỷ đồng, tăng 158% so với cùng kỳ.
Luỹ kế trong 9 tháng đầu năm 2026, Thép Nam Kim ghi nhận doanh thu đạt 12.884 tỷ đồng, tăng 10,4% so với cùng kỳ; lợi nhuận sau thuế đạt 252 tỷ đồng, tăng 124% so với cùng kỳ.
Trong năm 2026, Thép Nam Kim thông qua kế hoạch kinh doanh với tổng doanh thu 22.000 tỷ đồng, lợi nhuận trước thuế 400 tỷ đồng, lần lượt tăng 47,7% và 66,7% so với thực hiện trong năm 2025. Như vậy công ty đã hoàn thành 63% kế hoạch lợi nhuận cả năm.

articles.title: Eric Trump-backed robot soldier startup can't pay staff after founder borrowed $4.6 million from company to buy home
articles.text:
Foundation Future Industries, a maker of military humanoid robots advised and backed by Eric Trump, failed to pay employees last month as its cash reserves dwindled, according to people with direct knowledge of the matter.
Workers have yet to receive paychecks after San Francisco-based Foundation missed payroll on Oct. 30, said the people, who asked for anonymity to speak candidly about a private company.
The situation has particularly angered some inside the startup because its CEO and co-founder, Sankaet Pathak, borrowed $4.6 million from the company last year to buy a luxury home, money that could have been used to pay workers, the people said.
Public records show that an LLC that names Pathak as sole principal purchased a $4.6 million Sausalito, California, property with "sweeping, cinematic views" of the San Francisco Bay in October 2025.
A spokesman for Pathak acknowledged receiving a detailed list of the major points from this story on Thursday, but didn't respond to requests for comment. Pathak's previous startup, a fintech firm named Synapse, collapsed in 2024, leaving thousands of Americans locked out of their savings accounts.
Foundation's cash crunch comes at a precarious moment for the company, which Pathak has said is close to unveiling a next-generation, weapons-ready robot that will help the U.S. compete against Chinese rivals. At the same time, Pathak is seeking to raise hundreds of millions of dollars in funding at a $3 billion valuation.
The company has garnered headlines this year for Pathak's claims that his robots could soon take on battlefield tasks in Ukraine or patrol the U.S. border with Mexico. Broadcast interviews and articles about Foundation also include claims that the company has won $24 million in Pentagon contracts.
"What we're about to unveil in the next couple of months [is] going to be the strongest humanoid robot that exists anywhere in the world, including China," Pathak said in an April television interview.
'Plain sight'
That April interview introduced Eric Trump, the son of the U.S. president, as a Foundation investor and chief strategy advisor. It is unclear how large his stake is.
Eric Trump and his brother Donald Trump Jr. have invested in an array of defense firms, including makers of military drones and autonomous weapons. A July Washington Post investigation found that startups backed by investment vehicles linked to the brothers had secured at least $3.2 billion in government business.
"We have to win robotics in the United States of America," Eric Trump said in April. "When you go up and interact with these robots ... they fist bump you, they high five you, they follow your commands."
Eric Trump's involvement in Foundation drew the swift ire of Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who asked whether Foundation won U.S. defense contracts because of nepotism.
"Eric Trump went on FOX to brag about winning ANOTHER multimillion-dollar contract from the Trump administration," Warren said in an April 23 social media post. "This looks like corruption in plain sight."
Eric Trump didn't respond to requests for comment. His spokesperson recently told the Financial Times that Eric Trump had "no involvement in Foundation's management, operations, strategic decisions or commercial activities, including the solicitation, negotiation, procurement or execution of any government contracts."
While the Eric Trump announcement created speculation within Foundation that a Democratic-led Congress may look to investigate the company, Foundation itself didn't actually win the $24 million in contracts, despite that assertion being widely reported across news outlets.
Instead, it acquired Florida-based Boardwalk Robotics in late 2024, and government research contracts won by that firm account for the claim, said a person with knowledge of the matter. Foundation used Boardwalk's robot Alex as the basis for its first robot, the Phantom MK-1, this person said.
Foundation's deal for Boardwalk included performance milestones for the robot that haven't been reached, said a separate person with direct knowledge of the deal.
In 2024, CNBC reported that letters Pathak sent to prospective investors cited an imminent investment and $300 million purchase order from General Motors, claims the automaker rejected.
Foundation co-founder Mike LeBlanc said at the time he was "embarrassed" about the marketing materials.
Rescue loan?
Insiders fret that Foundation could soon fold if Pathak doesn't secure fresh funding. Pathak has been seeking to raise hundreds of millions of dollars at a $3 billion valuation since at least January.
Pathak is Foundation's sole board member, a structure that has raised concerns among prospective investors about corporate governance, said the people familiar with the matter. He also owns most of the firm's shares.
That setup allowed Pathak to borrow $4.6 million last year, which he called a short-term loan at the time, the people said. Existing investors are aware of the loan through the company's financial disclosures, the people said.
"This is what happens in a company with no governance," said one of the people. "Are you just going to let it ride into the ground, and you ride off into the sunset?"
Foundation also ran out of cash for payroll in August, though employees only had to wait about two days to get paid after the company secured a bridge loan from an existing investor, the people said.
Pathak told employees this week in a memo that he was working on sourcing money to pay back wages.
The company was founded in April 2024 by Pathak, Tribe Capital CEO Arjun Sethi and LeBlanc, co-founder of Cobalt Robotics, a maker of autonomous security guards, according to a fundraising pitch at the time.
Foundation went on to hire dozens of robotics engineers and artificial intelligence experts, managing to lure some from Tesla and Amazon-owned autonomous vehicle company Zoox.
Missing money
Before Foundation, Pathak was known as the founder of Synapse, a kind of middleman that enabled fintech firms like Mercury, Dave and YieldStreet to offer savings accounts and credit cards with the help of small community banks.
Synapse was a behind-the-scenes player until its collapse left more than 100,000 Americans with a combined $265 million in deposits locked out of their FDIC-backed accounts.
While some customers received partial payments during Synapse's bankruptcy proceedings, thousands remain without access to their money after more than two years. A bankruptcy trustee, the former FDIC chair Jelena McWilliams, said as much as $96 million in customer funds went missing.
The bankruptcy proceedings concluded last year without uncovering where the funds went; Pathak blamed a banking partner named Evolve, and Evolve blamed Synapse for the mess. U.S. regulators didn't intervene until the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau sued Synapse last year, opening up a $55 million fund for customer relief.
Pathak withdrew $320,000 in loans from Synapse as it spiraled toward bankruptcy in 2024 amid disputes over unmatched ledgers, according to the consultant and independent journalist Jason Mikula.
Federal prosecutors convened a grand jury to investigate possible criminal misconduct at Synapse, the Wall Street Journal reported last year. The WSJ report didn't mention Pathak specifically.
The controversy didn't dissuade Eric Trump from investing in Foundation and Pathak, who he called a friend in the April broadcast interview.
"I walked into his factory, and I couldn't believe what I saw," Eric Trump said. "I'm telling you, he's doing a phenomenal job."

articles.text:
Giá xe VinFast VF 6 mới nhất tháng 11/2026
Bảng giá xe VinFast VF 6 mới nhất tháng 11/2026 - giá niêm yết mới nhất của xe VinFast VF 6.

- 12-11-2026Đây là VinFast VF 6 mới: Tay nắm cửa bán ẩn, tầm hoạt động 510 km, giá từ 646 triệu
VF 6 là mẫu SUV điện được VinFast giới thiệu lần đầu tại khuôn khổ Triển lãm Điện tử Tiêu dùng - CES 2022 (Mỹ), diễn ra từ ngày 05/01/2022 - 08/01/2022. Xe ra mắt khách hàng quê nhà vào ngày 29/9/2023.
VinFast VF 6 có 5 màu ngoại thất là: trắng, đen, bạc, xanh, đỏ, xanh blue. Nội thất xe có 2 tùy chọn màu là nâu và đen.
Cũng được tạo nên bởi 2 studio nổi tiếng thế giới là Pininfarina và Torino Design, VinFast VF 6 mang vẻ đẹp của sự hiện đại, đề cao tính thẩm mỹ, đậm khí động học với những đường nét cá tính độc đáo.
Đầu xe nổi bật với dải đèn định vị LED tạo hình cánh chim, có thể phát sáng và bao trọn logo thương hiệu. Thân xe có nhiều đường nét bo tròn hơn là góc cạnh, tạo nên vẻ đẹp có phần “hiền lành”. Điểm nhấn ở đây là bộ la-zăng 5 chấu phối 2 tông màu trẻ trung, thể thao.
Đuôi xe VinFast VF 6 tiếp tục xuất hiện những điểm thiết kế mang tính nhận diện thương hiệu như dải LED đỏ tạo hình chữ V lớn, trải rộng sang hết 2 bên hông xe.
Khoang cabin của VinFast VF 6 thiết kế theo phong cách tối giản với điểm nhấn tại khu vực táp-lô chính là màn hình giải trí trung tâm kích thước lớn, hướng hẳn về phía người lái.
Vô-lăng 3 chấu thiết kế dạng D-cut thể thao, được nhấn nhá bởi các chi tiết mạ bạc. Cần số dạng nút bấm.
Ghế ngồi trên xe được bọc da. Nhờ ưu điểm không nhiều chi tiết cơ khí phức tạp, không gian nội thất của VF 6 rộng rãi ở cả hai hàng ghế.
VinFast trang bị cho VF 6 một môtơ điện ở trục trước. Bản Base công suất 174 mã lực, mô-men xoắn 250 Nm và bản Plus công suất 201 mã lực, mô-men xoắn 310 Nm.
Pin hai bản này dùng chung loại 59,6 kWh, phạm vi hoạt động 399 km bản Base và 381 km trên bản Plus. VF 6 là mẫu xe đầu tiên lắp pin do VinES sản xuất, với công nghệ cell pin hợp tác với Gotion (Trung Quốc).
VF 6 được trang bị các tính năng hỗ trợ lái ADAS cho cả 2 phiên bản Eco và Plus cùng các tính năng hiện đại như: Hỗ trợ lái trên đường cao tốc (Level 2); Kiểm soát đi giữa làn; Giám sát hành trình thích ứng; Hỗ trợ giữ làn khẩn cấp...
